(1964) | | _**Out to Lunch!**_ is a 1964 album by the American jazz multi-instrumentalist [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy"). His only recording on [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") as a leader, it was issued posthumously as BLP 4163 and BST 84163. Featuring Dolphy in a quintet with trumpeter [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), vibraphonist [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), bassist [Richard Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Davis_(bassist) "Richard Davis (bassist)"), and drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"), it is considered by critics as one of the finest albums issued on Blue Note and one of the high points of 1960s [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-aaj-2) [Reid Miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reid_Miles "Reid Miles")' cover artwork features a photo of a "Will Be Back" sign displayed in a shop window showing a seven-handed clock. ## Background \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Out_to_Lunch!&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Background")\] Dolphy declared in the album's liner notes that "Everyone's a leader in this session",[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) and he was fortunate to be joined by four sympathetic musicians, three of whom had previously performed and recorded with him. [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard") had roomed with Dolphy when they both first arrived in New York,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-4) and was featured on _[Outward Bound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Outward Bound (Eric Dolphy album)")_ (1960), Dolphy's debut as a leader. Dolphy and Hubbard had also appeared together on [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman")'s 1961 album _[Free Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_. [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson") had participated in the July 1963 recording sessions that produced Dolphy's albums _[Iron Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Man_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Iron Man (Eric Dolphy album)")_ and _[Conversations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversations_(Eric_Dolphy_album) "Conversations (Eric Dolphy album)")_. Dolphy expressed his excitement regarding the opportunity to work with Hutcherson again: "Bobby's vibes have a freer, more open sound than a piano. Pianos seem to control you, Bobby's vibes seems to open you up."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) Bassist [Richard Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Davis_(bassist) "Richard Davis (bassist)") had also participated in the July 1963 sessions, during which he recorded three duets with Dolphy ("Come Sunday", "Ode to Charlie Parker", and "Alone Together"). Davis was also the bassist on Dolphy and [Booker Little](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_Little "Booker Little")’s dates [at the Five Spot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_the_Five_Spot "At the Five Spot") in 1961. One reviewer stated that the pair "had one of the more meaningful connections in jazz; they communicated almost telepathically, as if completing each other's thoughts."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-5) Dolphy commented that "Richard doesn't play the usual bass lines. He plays rhythm with his lines. He leads you somewhere else."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) Drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"), credited as "Anthony Williams" on the album, had joined [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")' " [second great quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#1963%E2%80%931968:_Second_quintet "Miles Davis")" in May 1963, and turned eighteen only in December of that year. Regarding Williams, Dolphy stated that he "doesn't play time, he plays pulse."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) Dolphy biographers Vladimir Simosko and Barry Tepperman praised the musical chemistry of this group, observing that "the other musicians match and support \[Dolphy's\] conception with a truly fantastic sense of freedom and interplay."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-bio80-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-bio81-7) Roughly a month after the _Out to Lunch!_ session, Dolphy, Davis, and Williams participated in the recording of [Andrew Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Hill_(jazz_musician) "Andrew Hill (jazz musician)")'s _[Point of Departure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_of_Departure_(Andrew_Hill_album) "Point of Departure (Andrew Hill album)")_. Shortly afterwards, he moved to Europe following the completion of a European tour with [Charles Mingus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus "Charles Mingus"): "Why? Because I can get more work there playing my own music, and because if you try to do anything different in this country, people put you down for it."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-liner-3) Dolphy died from a [diabetic coma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabetic_coma "Diabetic coma") in [West Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Berlin "West Berlin") on June 29, 1964, at the age of 36.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_to_Lunch!#cite_note-8) ## Music \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Out_to_Lunch!&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Music")\] [... middle omitted — see footer ...] Retrieved from " [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Out\_to\_Lunch!&oldid=1365487194](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Out_to_Lunch!&oldid=1365487194)" [Categories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Category "Help:Category"): - - [Booker Little](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_Little "Booker Little") | | | | Website | [www.bluenote.com/artist/eric-dolphy/](http://www.bluenote.com/artist/eric-dolphy/) | | | | Education | [Los Angeles City College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_City_College "Los Angeles City College") | | | Musical artist **Eric Allan Dolphy Jr.** (June 20, 1928 – June 29, 1964) was an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") multi-instrumentalist, composer, and bandleader. Primarily an [alto saxophonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_saxophone "Alto saxophone"), [bass clarinetist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_clarinet "Bass clarinet"), and [flautist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flute "Flute"),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-baker-1) Dolphy was one of several multi-instrumentalists to gain prominence during the same era. His use of the bass clarinet helped to establish the unconventional instrument within jazz.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-am_guide-3) Dolphy extended the vocabulary and boundaries of the alto saxophone, and was among the earliest significant jazz flute soloists.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-4)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-am_guide-3) His [improvisational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") style was characterized by the use of wide [intervals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_(music) "Interval (music)"), in addition to employing an array of [extended techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_techniques "Extended techniques") to emulate the sounds of human voices and animals.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-gioiahist-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-feather-7) He used melodic lines that were "angular, zigzagging from interval to interval, taking hairpin turns at unexpected junctures, making dramatic leaps from the lower to the upper register."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-gioiahist-6) Although Dolphy's work is sometimes classified as [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), his compositions and solos were often rooted in conventional (if highly abstracted) tonal [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") harmony.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-10) ## Early life, family and education [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Eric_Dolphy_-_Dorsey_-_1947.jpg/250px-Eric_Dolphy_-_Dorsey_-_1947.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eric_Dolphy_-_Dorsey_-_1947.jpg) Dolphy's senior high school class portrait (1947) Eric Allan Dolphy Jr. was born on June 20, 1928, in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), where he was raised.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-sparked-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Ratliff-12) His parents, Sadie and Eric Sr.,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-13) had immigrated to the United States from [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-baker-1) He began music lessons at the age of six, studying clarinet and saxophone privately.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_76-14) While still in junior high school, he began to study the oboe, aspiring to a professional symphonic career,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_76-14) and received a two-year scholarship to study at the music school of the [University of Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southern_California "University of Southern California").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-Ratliff-12) When aged 13, he received a "Superior" award on clarinet from the California School Band and Orchestra festival.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_76-14) He attended [Susan Miller Dorsey High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Miller_Dorsey_High_School "Susan Miller Dorsey High School") in Los Angeles, where he continued his musical studies and learned additional instruments.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_76-14) By 1946, he was co-director of the Youth Choir at the Westminster Presbyterian Church run by Reverend Hampton B. Hawes, father of the [jazz pianist of the same name.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampton_Hawes "Hampton Hawes")[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_76-14) He graduated from high school in 1947 and attended [Los Angeles City College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_City_College "Los Angeles City College"), during which time he played contemporary classical works such as [Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stravinsky "Stravinsky")'s _[L'Histoire du soldat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Histoire_du_soldat "L'Histoire du soldat")_ and, along with [Jimmy Knepper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Knepper "Jimmy Knepper") and [Art Farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Farmer "Art Farmer"), performed with [Roy Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Porter_(drummer) "Roy Porter (drummer)")'s _17 Beboppers_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-thomas_76-14) He went on to make eight recordings with Porter by 1949.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy#cite_note-baker-1) On these early sessions, Dolphy occasionally played [baritone saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baritone_saxophone "Baritone saxophone"), as well as [alto saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_saxophone "Alto saxophone"), flute, and [soprano clarinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soprano_clarinet "Soprano clarinet"). - [experimental rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_rock "Experimental rock") | | Cultural origins | Late 1960s, [Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury "Canterbury"), England | | Other topics | | - [Rock in Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_in_Opposition "Rock in Opposition") | The **Canterbury scene** (or **Canterbury sound**) is a musical scene that originated in the city of [Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury "Canterbury"), [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent "Kent"), England during the late 1960s and early 1970s.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-All-1) Associated with [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-O'Dair2015-2) the term describes a loosely defined, [improvisational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation") style that blended elements of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), and [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-All-1) The Canterbury scene was born from the ashes of [The Wilde Flowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wilde_Flowers "The Wilde Flowers"), a psych-pop outfit active in the mid to late 60s. After the band broke up in 1969, its members soon went on to play together in numerous bands (e.g. [Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine"), [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(band) "Caravan (band)"), [Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gong_(band) "Gong (band)"), [Hatfield and the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatfield_and_the_North "Hatfield and the North"), [Egg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egg_(band) "Egg (band)"), and [National Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health "National Health")), with ever-changing and overlapping personnel, creating some similarities in their musical output [\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-ProgArchives-3). Many prominent British [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") or [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") musicians began their career in Canterbury bands, including [Hugh Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Hopper "Hugh Hopper"), [Steve Hillage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Hillage "Steve Hillage"), [Dave Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Stewart_(musician,_born_1950) "Dave Stewart (musician, born 1950)"), [Robert Wyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wyatt "Robert Wyatt"), [Kevin Ayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Ayers "Kevin Ayers"), [Richard Sinclair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Sinclair "Richard Sinclair"), [Tony Coe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Coe "Tony Coe"), [Daevid Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daevid_Allen "Daevid Allen"), and [Mike Ratledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Ratledge "Mike Ratledge").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-AM-CS-4) ## Definition and history The Canterbury scene is largely defined by a set of musicians and bands with intertwined members. These are not tied by very strong musical similarities, but a certain whimsicality, touches of [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelia "Psychedelia"), rather abstruse lyrics, and a use of [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation") derived from [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") are common elements in their work.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-AM-CS-4) "The real essence of 'Canterbury Sound' is the tension between complicated harmonies, extended improvisations, and the sincere desire to write catchy pop songs." "In the very best Canterbury music...the musically silly and the musically serious are juxtaposed in an amusing and endearing way."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-5) There is variation within the scene, for example from pop/rock like early [Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine") and much [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(band) "Caravan (band)") to avant-garde composed pieces as with early [National Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health "National Health") to improvised jazz as with later Soft Machine or [In Cahoots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Cahoots "In Cahoots"). [Didier Malherbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didier_Malherbe "Didier Malherbe") (of [Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gong_(band) "Gong (band)")) has defined the scene as having "certain chord changes, in particular the use of minor second chords, certain harmonic combinations, and a great clarity in the aesthetics, and a way of improvising that is very different from what is done in jazz."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-whatis-6) There is debate about the existence and definition of the scene. [Dave Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Stewart_(musician,_born_1950) "Dave Stewart (musician, born 1950)") has complained at the nomenclature as he and many other musicians identified with the Canterbury scene never had anything to do with Canterbury, the place. The former Soft Machine bassist [Hugh Hopper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Hopper "Hugh Hopper"), who lived in [Whitstable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitstable "Whitstable"), near Canterbury, said: "I think it's a rather artificial label, a journalistic thing... I don't mind it, but people like [Robert \[Wyatt\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wyatt "Robert Wyatt"), he in fact hates that idea, because he was born somewhere else and just happened to go to school here. In the time when [the Wilde Flowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wilde_Flowers "The Wilde Flowers") started we hardly ever worked in Canterbury. It wasn't until Robert and [Daevid \[Allen\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daevid_Allen "Daevid Allen") went to London to start Soft Machine that anything happened at all. They weren't really a Canterbury band \[...\] if it helps people understand or listen to more music then it is fine."[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-whatis-6) In the 21st century, the Canterbury group [Syd Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_Arthur "Syd Arthur") have been seen as latter-day practitioners.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-7) ## Others Poet, painter, and singer [Lady June](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_June "Lady June") was regarded an "honorary member" of the Canterbury scene for having performed and recorded with some of the members, and being a "landlady" to many in her flat in [Maida Vale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maida_Vale "Maida Vale"), London.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_scene#cite_note-9) ## References 1. # Spontaneous composition Spontaneous composition | | | | --- | --- | | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/120px-Question_book-new.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg) | This article **needs additional citations for [verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Please help [improve this article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Spontaneous_composition "Special:EditPage/Spontaneous composition") by [adding citations to reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners "Help:Referencing for beginners"). Unsourced material may be challenged and removed.
_Find sources:_ ["Spontaneous composition"](https://www.google.com/search?as_eq=wikipedia&q=%22Spontaneous+composition%22)– [news](https://www.google.com/search?tbm=nws&q=%22Spontaneous+composition%22+-wikipedia&tbs=ar:1) **·** [newspapers](https://www.google.com/search?&q=%22Spontaneous+composition%22&tbs=bkt:s&tbm=bks) **·** [books](https://www.google.com/search?tbs=bks:1&q=%22Spontaneous+composition%22+-wikipedia) **·** [scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Spontaneous+composition%22) **·** [JSTOR](https://www.jstor.org/action/doBasicSearch?Query=%22Spontaneous+composition%22&acc=on&wc=on)_(June 2009)__([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ | **Spontaneous composition** is [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music") performed, occurring, or resulting from a sudden natural impulse, tendency, or inclination; without effort or premeditation; natural and unconstrained; unplanned.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-1) Spontaneity in music is mostly associated with [improvised music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") and jazz, but through the course of the last century it became practiced in other genres as well. [Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") is one possible [compositional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_composition "Musical composition") tool used in creating a **spontaneous composition**.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-2) Keith Jarrett, an American pianist, is known for his work, which is almost exclusively based on improvisation. Keith Jarrett considers spontaneity to be an essential element of his music. He never writes musical notations for his works and makes no plans before a performance. Jarrett describes his compositional process as “being three people at once while improvising: the Improviser, the Spontaneous Composer, and the Keyboardist (the man at the keyboard). Jarrett himself is performing all of the tasks he describes simultaneously, but in an attempt to explain improvisation as an activity, he breaks down the task of performing into separate but interdependent “jobs” completed by his personae. (…) Jarrett describes the perfect work of his personae as the height of improvisational experience; when each of his personae are able to work freely and in harmony with the others (…).”[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-3) Jarrett further explains: "If I remain the listener and not think I'm the player, if I remain the listener and not control the thing, something happens."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-4) The term "spontaneous composition" is closely associated with the music of Art Ensemble of Chicago. The band is best known for their innovative combining of absolute free playing with composed parts, building their compositions on improvisation, augmented communication between the players and prearranged sequences. Their music is often associated with avant-garde jazz, but they played freely through various musical zones, from the most reverent, like traditional, gospel, or so-called “Great Black Music”, to the most radical, like free-jazz or experimental. However, they never confined themselves to a single musical style or strict rules. They simply called it “creative music”.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-5) Unlike Keith Jarrett's compositions, which were created entirely spontaneously, the music of Art Ensemble of Chicago was built through various combinations in the range between free and prearranged music. Its member, Roscoe Mitchell, multi-instrumentalist and inventor of new percussions, describes their way of composing as follows: ”I’m interested in all aspects of creativity. And one goal has always been to be a really good improviser who really does create spontaneous composition. So I study all the time, trying to develop ways to improve communication amongst the players and to shape and control the improvisations. There are so many paths to investigate, and not just contemporary paths.”[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-6) [Scott Barry Kaufman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Barry_Kaufman "Scott Barry Kaufman"), a psychologist known for his work on creativity, human potential and intelligence, explores concepts related to spontaneity in creative processes. He postulates that spontaneity is essential for creative process and he analyzed it by exploring processes like improvisation, brainstorming, openness, or playfulness.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_composition#cite_note-7) ## References 1. [Jump to content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#bodyContent) From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (Redirected from [Backbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Backbeat&redirect=no "Backbeat")) Basic unit of time in music and music theory For other uses, see [beat music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_music "Beat music"), [beat (acoustics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(acoustics) "Beat (acoustics)"), [drum beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_beat "Drum beat"), and [beat (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(disambiguation) "Beat (disambiguation)"). [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Metric_levels.svg/500px-Metric_levels.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Metric_levels.svg) Metric levels: beat level shown in middle with division levels above and multiple levels below. In [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music") and [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory"), the **beat** is the basic unit of time, the [pulse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulse_(music) "Pulse (music)") (regularly repeating event), of the _mensural level_[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-1) (or _beat level_).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-2) The beat is often defined as the rhythm listeners would tap their toes to when listening to a piece of music, or the numbers a musician [counts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counting_(music) "Counting (music)") while performing, though in practice this may be technically incorrect (often the first multiple level).\[ _[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] In popular use, _beat_ can refer to a variety of related concepts, including [pulse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulse_(music) "Pulse (music)"), [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo"), [meter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meter_(music) "Meter (music)"), specific [rhythms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm "Rhythm"), and [groove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groove_(popular_music) "Groove (popular music)"). Rhythm in music is characterized by a repeating sequence of [stressed and unstressed beats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#On-beat_and_off-beat) (often called "strong" and "weak") and divided into [bars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_(music) "Bar (music)") organized by [time signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_signature "Time signature") and [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo") indications. Beats are related to and distinguished from pulse, rhythm (grouping), and meter: > Meter is the measurement of the number of pulses between more or less regularly recurring accents. Therefore, in order for meter to exist, some of the pulses in a series must be accented—marked for consciousness—relative to others. When pulses are thus counted within a metric context, they are referred to as _beats_. — [Leonard B. Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_B._Meyer "Leonard B. Meyer") and [Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grosvenor_Cooper?action=edit&redlink=1 "Grosvenor Cooper (page does not exist)") (1960)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-3) [Metric levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meter_(music)#Metric_structure "Meter (music)") faster than the beat level are division levels, and slower levels are multiple levels. Beat has always been an important part of music. Some [music genres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre "Music genre") such as [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") will in general de-emphasize the beat, while others such as [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco "Disco") emphasize the beat to accompany dance.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-hhd-4) ## Division \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beat_(music)&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Division")\] Main article: [Metre (music) §Metric structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre_(music)#Metric_structure "Metre (music)") As beats are combined to form measures, each beat is divided into parts. The nature of this combination and division is what determines meter. Music where two beats are combined is in [duple meter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duple_meter "Duple meter"), music where three beats are combined is in [triple meter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_meter "Triple meter"). Music where the beat is split in two are in simple meter, music where the beat is split in three are called compound meter. Thus, simple duple (**2** **4**, **4** **4**, etc.), simple triple (**3** **4**), compound duple (**6** **8**), and compound triple (**9** **8**). Divisions which require numbers, [tuplets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuplet "Tuplet") (for example, dividing a [quarter note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarter_note "Quarter note") into five equal parts), are irregular divisions and subdivisions. Subdivision begins two levels below the beat level: starting with a quarter note or a dotted quarter note, subdivision begins when the note is divided into sixteenth notes. ## Downbeat and upbeat \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beat_(music)&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Downbeat and upbeat")\] [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/65/Anacrusis-bwv736.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anacrusis-bwv736.png) Beginning of [Bach's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach") [BWV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BWV "BWV") 736, with upbeat (anacrusis) in red. [Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/4/41/Anacrusis-bwv736.mid/Anacrusis-bwv736.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anacrusis-bwv736.mid "File:Anacrusis-bwv736.mid") The _downbeat_ is the first beat of the [bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_(music) "Bar (music)"), i.e. number 1. The _upbeat_ is the last beat in the previous bar which immediately precedes, and hence anticipates, the downbeat.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-Groveupbeat-5) Both terms correspond to the direction taken by the hand of a [conductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_(music) "Conductor (music)"). > This idea of directionality of beats is significant when you translate its effect on music. The crusis of a measure or a phrase is a beginning; it propels sound and energy forward, so the sound needs to lift and have forward motion to create a sense of direction. The anacrusis leads to the crusis, but doesn't have the same 'explosion' of sound; it serves as a preparation for the crusis.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-6) An anticipatory note or succession of notes occurring before the first barline of a piece is sometimes referred to as an upbeat figure, section or phrase. Alternative expressions include "pickup" and " [anacrusis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anacrusis "Anacrusis")" (the latter ultimately from Greek _ana_ \["up towards"\] and _krousis_ \["strike"/"impact"\] through French _anacrouse_). In English, _anákrousis_ translates literally as "pushing up". The term anacrusis was borrowed from the field of [poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry "Poetry"), in which it refers to one or more unstressed extrametrical [syllables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllable "Syllable") at the beginning of a line.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#cite_note-Groveupbeat-5) ## On-beat and off-beat \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beat_(music)&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: On-beat and off-beat")\] ![\version "2.22.0" \header { tagline = ##f} \score { \drums \with {midiInstrument = "drums"} \with { \numericTimeSignature } { \repeat volta 2 {\stemUp r4 sne8 sne8 r4 sne r4 sne8 sne8 r4 sne \break } } \layout {} } \score { \unfoldRepeats { \drums \with {midiInstrument = "drums"}{ \repeat volta 2 { r4 sne8 sne8 r4 sne r4 sne8 sne8 r4 sne } } } \midi { \tempo 4 = 100 } }](https://upload.wikimedia.org/score/s/7/s7acmq8uo5ryq1hjhewwyzjrppdrfaf/s7acmq8u.svg) Audio playback is not supported in your browser. [Jump to content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#bodyContent) From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia German independent record label Record label | ECM Records | | --- | | [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/ECM_Records.svg/250px-ECM_Records.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ECM_Records.svg) | | Founded | 1969(1969) | | Founder | [Manfred Eicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Eicher "Manfred Eicher") | | Distributor | [Universal Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music "Universal Music") | | Genre | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"), [world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music") | | Country of origin | [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") | | Location | [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich") | | Official website | [ecmrecords.com](http://ecmrecords.com/) | **ECM** (Edition of Contemporary Music) is an independent [record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label") founded by Karl Egger, [Manfred Eicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Eicher "Manfred Eicher") and Manfred Scheffner in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich") in 1969. While ECM is best known for [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") music, the label has released a variety of recordings, and ECM's artists often refuse to acknowledge boundaries between genres. ECM's motto is "the most beautiful sound next to silence", taken from a 1971 review of ECM releases in _[Coda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coda_(magazine) "Coda (magazine)")_, a Canadian jazz magazine.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-1) ECM has been distributed in the U.S. by [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records"), [PolyGram Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PolyGram_Records "PolyGram Records"), [BMG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertelsmann_Music_Group "Bertelsmann Music Group"), and, since 1999, [Universal Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music "Universal Music"), the successor of PolyGram, worldwide. Its album covers were profiled in two books: _Sleeves of Desire_ and _Windfall Light_, both published by Lars Müller. ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ECM_Records&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] The first ECM release produced by Manfred Scheffner was pianist [Mal Waldron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mal_Waldron "Mal Waldron")'s 1969 recording _[Free at Last](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_at_Last_(Mal_Waldron_album) "Free at Last (Mal Waldron album)")_. The label went on to release recordings by many prominent jazz musicians, including [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley"), [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette"), [Keith Jarrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett "Keith Jarrett"), [Jan Garbarek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Garbarek "Jan Garbarek"), [Pat Metheny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Metheny "Pat Metheny"), [Gary Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Burton "Gary Burton"), [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), [John Abercrombie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Abercrombie_(guitarist) "John Abercrombie (guitarist)"), [Dave Liebman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Liebman "Dave Liebman"), [Eberhard Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eberhard_Weber "Eberhard Weber"), [Egberto Gismonti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egberto_Gismonti "Egberto Gismonti"), [Dave Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Holland_(bassist) "Dave Holland (bassist)"), [Terje Rypdal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terje_Rypdal "Terje Rypdal"), [Stefano Bollani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefano_Bollani "Stefano Bollani") and [Ralph Towner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Towner "Ralph Towner"). The label has also released recordings in the [world music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music") genre by artists including [Steve Tibbetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Tibbetts "Steve Tibbetts"), [Stephan Micus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephan_Micus "Stephan Micus"), [Codona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona "Codona"), [Anouar Brahem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anouar_Brahem "Anouar Brahem"), [L. Shankar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L._Shankar "L. Shankar"), [Jon Hassell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Hassell "Jon Hassell"), and [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos"). Manfred Eicher continues to take an active interest in the music released by ECM, acting as [producer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_producer "Record producer") of the vast majority of its recordings, although Steve Lake, Thomas Stoewsand, Robert Hurwitz, Lee Townsend, Hans Wendl and Sun Chung have also produced discs for the label. The typical ECM session is just three days: two days to record, one day to [mix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_mixing_(recorded_music) "Audio mixing (recorded music)"). Many of the albums have been recorded with [Jan Erik Kongshaug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Erik_Kongshaug "Jan Erik Kongshaug") (of Talent Studios and later Rainbow Studios) in Oslo, Norway, as sound engineer; other engineers have included Martin Wieland (who recorded Jarrett's "The Köln Concert"), James Farber, Stefano Amerio and, on classical recordings, Peter Laenger. ### New Series and commemorative editions \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ECM_Records&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: New Series and commemorative editions")\] The _ECM New Series_ was created in 1984 to document Western classical works. It has released works by composers from the early ( [Thomas Tallis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Tallis "Thomas Tallis"), [Carlo Gesualdo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlo_Gesualdo "Carlo Gesualdo"), [Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Pierluigi_da_Palestrina "Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina")) to the contemporary ( [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage"), [Elliott Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliott_Carter "Elliott Carter"), [Steve Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Reich "Steve Reich") and [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams_(composer) "John Adams (composer)")). The series was initiated for [Arvo Pärt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arvo_P%C3%A4rt "Arvo Pärt")'s record debut _Tabula Rasa_, which Eicher recorded and produced in 1977, 1983, and 1984. Since then Pärt and Eicher have built a strong relationship: all works premiere on recordings for the label and all are done in presence of the composer. Keith Jarrett, better known as a jazz musician, contributed together with [Gidon Kremer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gidon_Kremer "Gidon Kremer") amongst others to _Tabula Rasa_. He later recorded several classical works by [Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach"), [Mozart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart "Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart"), [Shostakovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Shostakovich "Dmitri Shostakovich"), and others for the series. The three albums _[Music for 18 Musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_for_18_Musicians "Music for 18 Musicians")_, _[Octet/Music for a Large Ensemble/Violin Phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octet/Music_for_a_Large_Ensemble/Violin_Phase "Octet/Music for a Large Ensemble/Violin Phase")_, and _[Tehillim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tehillim_(Reich) "Tehillim (Reich)")_ by Reich were recorded before 1984 (all with the composer performing) and were later moved to the classical department together with some by [Meredith Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meredith_Monk "Meredith Monk"), [Thomas Demenga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Demenga "Thomas Demenga") and [Harald Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Weiss "Harald Weiss").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records#cite_note-2) Several of John Adams' works from his minimalist period have been released through the label as well, including _[Harmonium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonium_(Adams) "Harmonium (Adams)")_ and _[Harmonielehre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonielehre "Harmonielehre")_. [Jump to content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#bodyContent) From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (Redirected from [ESP-Disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ESP-Disk&redirect=no "ESP-Disk")) American record company and label Record label | ESP-Disk' | | --- | | [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/3/38/Esp-disk-logo.jpg/120px-Esp-disk-logo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Esp-disk-logo.jpg) | | Founded | 1963(1963) | | Founder | [Bernard Stollman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Stollman "Bernard Stollman") | | Genre | [Free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [free improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation"), [folk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_rock "Folk rock"), [underground rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_rock "Underground rock") | | Country of origin | U.S. | | Location | [Brooklyn, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn,_New_York "Brooklyn, New York") | | Official website | [www.espdisk.com](http://www.espdisk.com/) | **ESP-Disk'** is a New York–based record company and [label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label") founded in 1963[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-1) by lawyer [Bernard Stollman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Stollman "Bernard Stollman"). ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ESP-Disk%27&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Helix%2C_v.4%2C_no.6%2C_Aug._29%2C_1968_-_DPLA_-_73a8fb15a58855b090d500dba021b984_%28page_21%29.jpg/250px-Helix%2C_v.4%2C_no.6%2C_Aug._29%2C_1968_-_DPLA_-_73a8fb15a58855b090d500dba021b984_%28page_21%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Helix,_v.4,_no.6,_Aug._29,_1968_-_DPLA_-_73a8fb15a58855b090d500dba021b984_(page_21).jpg) A 1968 ad in Seattle underground paper _[Helix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helix_(newspaper) "Helix (newspaper)")_ offers a free ESP-Disk' with a year's subscription. Though it originally existed to release [Esperanto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esperanto "Esperanto")-based [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esperanto_music "Esperanto music"), beginning with its second release (Albert Ayler's _[Spiritual Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity "Spiritual Unity")_), ESP became the most important exponent of what is commonly referred to as [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-2) Early releases included albums by [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley"), [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders") and [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-3) ESP also released recordings by uncommercial [underground rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_rock "Underground rock") acts including [the Fugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fugs "The Fugs"), [The Godz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Godz_(New_York_band) "The Godz (New York band)") and [Pearls Before Swine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearls_Before_Swine_(band) "Pearls Before Swine (band)"). The label's motto is "The artists alone decide what you will hear."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-4) [Bernard Stollman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Stollman "Bernard Stollman") faced allegations of not paying [royalties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royalties "Royalties") to the artists that were signed to ESP-Disk'.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-5) [Tom Rapp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Rapp "Tom Rapp") of the band [Pearls Before Swine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearls_Before_Swine_(band) "Pearls Before Swine (band)") claimed that: "We never got any money from ESP. Never, not even like a hundred dollars or something. My real sense is that he \[Stollman\] was abducted by aliens, and when he was probed it erased his memory of where all the money was".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-6) [Peter Stampfel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Stampfel "Peter Stampfel") of the band [Holy Modal Rounders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Modal_Rounders "Holy Modal Rounders") and [The Fugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fugs "The Fugs") claimed that Stollman told him that "the contract says that all rights belong to me. You have no royalties ever, ever, ever. The publishing is mine. You don't own the songs anymore. We don't owe you anything".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-7) Members of The Fugs have also stated claims that they received an unfavourable record contract. [Ed Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Sanders "Ed Sanders") said that "our royalty rate was less than 3%, one of the lower percentages in the history of western civilization".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-8) _801 Magazine_, which featured an interview with Stollman in 2008, said that Stollman claimed that "he paid all the recording costs and gave the musicians small advances", and that "he never made any money from the music".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk%27#cite_note-9) ## Discography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ESP-Disk%27&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Discography")\] Main article: [ESP-Disk' discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk'_discography "ESP-Disk' discography") ## See also \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ESP-Disk%27&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: See also")\] - [BYG Actuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYG_Actuel "BYG Actuel") - [AACM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians "Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians") - [List of record labels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_record_labels "List of record labels") ## References \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=ESP-Disk%27&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: References")\] 1. [Jump to content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYG_Actuel#bodyContent) From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (Redirected from [BYG Actuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BYG_Actuel&redirect=no "BYG Actuel")) French jazz record label Record label | BYG Records | | --- | | Founded | 1967(1967) | | Founder | Jean Georgakarakos
Jean-Luc Young
Fernand Boruso | | Defunct | 1973(1973) | | Genre | [Free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [Avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") | | Country of origin | [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") | | Location | [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") | **BYG Records** was a French [record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label") known for the **Actuel** series specializing in [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"). However, the label released a handful of non-jazz recordings by artists such as [Musica Elettronica Viva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musica_Elettronica_Viva "Musica Elettronica Viva"), [Terry Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Riley "Terry Riley"), [Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_(band) "Freedom (band)") and [Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gong_(band) "Gong (band)"). ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=BYG_Records&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] BYG Records was founded in March 1967 by [Jean Georgakarakos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Georgakarakos "Jean Georgakarakos"), Jean-Luc Young, and Fernand Boruso. The name of the label was formed from the initial letters of the founders' surnames. Georgakarakos had previously established himself as a record distributor and importer, while Young worked for [Barclay Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barclay_Records "Barclay Records") and Boruso for [Saravah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saravah "Saravah"), the record label formed by Pierre Barouh. The label invited American free jazz musicians to [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") to record in the summer of 1969, a time when they were receiving little support or attention in the United States. Many of these musicians were already overseas at the time, having appeared at the Pan-African Music Festival in [Algiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algiers "Algiers") in July 1969.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYG_Actuel#cite_note-1) (Jazz photographer Jacques Bisceglia was largely responsible for connecting the label and musicians, and the "B" in BYG is often wrongly held to refer to Bisceglia.) The resulting albums are an important repository of free jazz recordings from the period. BYG Actuel was also responsible for organising the Actuel festival, which took place in late October 1969 in the small Belgian town of Amougies. The festival was initially intended to take place in or near Paris, but was banned by the French authorities. It featured many leading exponents of progressive rock, such as [Frank Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa "Frank Zappa"), [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd"), [Captain Beefheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Beefheart "Captain Beefheart"), [Soft Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine"), [Ten Years After](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ten_Years_After "Ten Years After"), [Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band) "Yes (band)") and [The Nice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nice "The Nice"). The festival was a popular success, with around 20,000 visitors over five nights, but it was a financial failure. In July 1970, Georgakarakos organised the Popanalia festival at Biot on the [French Riviera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Riviera "French Riviera"), but this was also financially unsuccessful. By 1972, financial problems had plagued BYG to the point where it virtually went underground. Georgakarakos and Young later formed their own record labels, [Celluloid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celluloid_Records "Celluloid Records") (Georgakarakos) and [Charly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charly_Records "Charly Records") (Young). In 2002 a compilation album featuring the best of the label, _JazzActuel: a collection of avant garde/free jazz/psychedelia from the BYG/Actuel catalogue of 1969–1971_, was released by Charly (as a 3-CD set) and Get Back Records of Italy (as a 6-LP set). The collection was curated by [Thurston Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thurston_Moore "Thurston Moore") of [Sonic Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_Youth "Sonic Youth") and journalist [Byron Coley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byron_Coley "Byron Coley").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYG_Actuel#cite_note-2) ## Discography \[ **India Navigation** was an American record company and [independent record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_record_label "Independent record label") that specialized in [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") in the 1970s and 1980s. It was founded by Bob Cummins, a corporate lawyer who helped jazz musicians with legal matters.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_Navigation#cite_note-Ratliff-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_Navigation#cite_note-New_Grove-2) Its catalogue included [Arthur Blythe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blythe "Arthur Blythe"), [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders"), [Hamiet Bluiett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiet_Bluiett "Hamiet Bluiett"), [Chico Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chico_Freeman "Chico Freeman"), [Cecil McBee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_McBee "Cecil McBee"), and the [Revolutionary Ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary_Ensemble "Revolutionary Ensemble").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_Navigation#cite_note-New_Grove-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_Navigation#cite_note-Jazz_House-3) In addition to this, some recordings of [minimal music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_music "Minimal music"), such as Arnold Dreyblatt, Phill Niblock and Joseph Celli, or Tom Johnson, also appeared.

# Prestige Records Prestige Records American jazz record label Not to be confused with the namesake Prestige Records, a British label that releases the work of [Imran Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imran_Khan_(singer) "Imran Khan (singer)"). Record label | Prestige Records | | --- | | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Prestige_Records_logo.svg/500px-Prestige_Records_logo.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prestige_Records_logo.svg) | | Parent company | [Concord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_(entertainment_company) "Concord (entertainment company)") | | Founded | 1949;76years ago(1949)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-1) | | Founder | [Bob Weinstock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Weinstock "Bob Weinstock") | | Genre | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") | | Country of origin | United States | | Location | [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") | | Official website | [concordmusicgroup.com/labels/Prestige](http://concordmusicgroup.com/labels/Prestige) | **Prestige Records** is a [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") record company and label founded in 1949 by [Bob Weinstock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Weinstock "Bob Weinstock") in New York City which issued recordings in the mainstream, bop, and cool jazz idioms.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-2) The company recorded hundreds of albums by many of the leading jazz musicians of the day, sometimes issuing them on subsidiary labels. The company's began releasing jazz records in 78 and 45 RPM formats in 1950. The Prestige label includes the 13000 and 25000 cat# series. Prestige International was a sub-label of Prestige, active from 1960 to 1969, that mostly released folk music. In 1971, the company was sold to [Fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_Records "Fantasy Records"), which was later absorbed by [Concord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Records "Concord Records"). ## History The Prestige office was located at 446 West 50th Street, [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-3) Its catalogue included [Gene Ammons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Ammons "Gene Ammons"), [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), [Stan Getz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Getz "Stan Getz"), [Wardell Gray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wardell_Gray "Wardell Gray"), [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk"), and [Sonny Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Rollins "Sonny Rollins").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-2) Audio engineer [Rudy Van Gelder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Van_Gelder "Rudy Van Gelder") was the recording engineer of many Prestige albums in the 1950s and early-to-mid-1960s. Prestige created new labels in 1960: Swingville, Moodsville, covering jazz, [Bluesville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluesville_Records "Bluesville Records") featuring blues revival artists, Lively Arts featuring spoken word recordings and Prestige International, Prestige Folklore, Irish and Near East with folk and world music.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-2) By the later 1950s, Weinstock ceased supervising recording sessions directly, employing [Chris Albertson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Albertson "Chris Albertson"), [Ozzie Cadena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzie_Cadena "Ozzie Cadena"), [Esmond Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esmond_Edwards "Esmond Edwards"), [Don Schlitten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Schlitten "Don Schlitten"), and producer/music supervisor [Bob Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Porter_(record_producer) "Bob Porter (record producer)"), among others, to fulfill this function.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-2) Musicians recording for the label in the 1960s included [Jaki Byard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaki_Byard "Jaki Byard") and [Booker Ervin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booker_Ervin "Booker Ervin"), while Prestige remained commercially viable by recording a number of [soul jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_jazz "Soul jazz") artists like [Charles Earland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Earland "Charles Earland"). In 1966 the company's headquarters were located at 203 South Washington Avenue in [Bergenfield, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergenfield,_New_Jersey "Bergenfield, New Jersey").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-4) The company was sold[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-label-5) to [Fantasy Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_Records "Fantasy Records") in 1971, and original releases on the label formed a significant proportion of its [Original Jazz Classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Original_Jazz_Classics "Original Jazz Classics") line. Fantasy was purchased by [Concord Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Records "Concord Records") in 2005.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-label-5) In 2017, Concord Music Group revived the Prestige label. The first album released under the label's reactivation was _A Social Call_ from Texas native [Jazzmeia Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazzmeia_Horn "Jazzmeia Horn").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records#cite_note-7) ## Discography Main article: [Prestige Records discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records_discography "Prestige Records discography") ## References 1. # Savoy Records Savoy Records American record label | | | | --- | --- | | [![icon](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/120px-Question_book-new.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg) | This article **needs additional citations for [verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Savoy disc from the 1940s | | Parent company | [Concord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_(entertainment_company) "Concord (entertainment company)") | | Founded | 1942;84years ago(1942) | | Founder | [Herman Lubinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Lubinsky "Herman Lubinsky") | | Distributor | [Universal Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group") | | Genre | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music") | | Country of origin | U.S. | | Location | [Newark, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark,_New_Jersey "Newark, New Jersey") | **Savoy Records** is an American record company and label established by [Herman Lubinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Lubinsky "Herman Lubinsky") in 1942 in Newark, New Jersey.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-1) Savoy specialized in [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), and [gospel music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music"). In September 2017, Savoy was acquired by [Concord Bicycle Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Bicycle_Music "Concord Bicycle Music").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-2) ## History In the 1940s, Savoy recorded some of the biggest names in jazz, including [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), [Erroll Garner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erroll_Garner "Erroll Garner"), [Dexter Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dexter_Gordon "Dexter Gordon"), [J. J. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Johnson "J. J. Johnson"), [Fats Navarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fats_Navarro "Fats Navarro"), and [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"). In 1948, it began buying other labels: Bop, [Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Records "Discovery Records"), [National](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Records "National Records"), and [Regent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regent_Records_(US) "Regent Records (US)"). It also reissued music from Jewel Records.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-New_Grove-1) In the early 1960s, Savoy briefly recorded several [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") artists. These included [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley"), [Bill Dixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Dixon "Bill Dixon"), [Charles Moffett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Moffett "Charles Moffett"), [Perry Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perry_Robinson "Perry Robinson"), [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp"), [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"), [Marzette Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marzette_Watts "Marzette Watts"), and [Valdo Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valdo_Williams "Valdo Williams"). After Lubinsky's death in 1974, [Clive Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Davis "Clive Davis"), then manager of [Arista Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arista_Records "Arista Records"), acquired Savoy's catalogue. After that, [Joe Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Fields_(producer) "Joe Fields (producer)") of [Muse Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muse_Records "Muse Records") purchased the catalogue from Arista. In 1986, [Malaco Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaco_Records "Malaco Records") acquired Savoy's black gospel titles and contracts.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-3) In 1991, [Nippon Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nippon_Columbia "Nippon Columbia") acquired Savoy and its library, and distributed Savoy releases through its wholly owned subsidiary, Savoy Jazz. In 2003, Savoy Jazz acquired the rights to the [Muse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muse_Records "Muse Records") and [Landmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landmark_Records "Landmark Records") catalogues from [32 Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32_Jazz "32 Jazz").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-porter-4) In 2009, the label entered a distribution arrangement with [Warner Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Music_Group "Warner Music Group").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-wmg-5) Savoy included the rock imprint [429 Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/429_Records "429 Records"). Many of the label's African American artists begrudged the label's founder, Herman Lubinsky, feeling underpaid for their work. Tiny Price, a journalist for the African American newspaper _The Newark Herald News_, said of Savoy and Lubinsky: > There's no doubt everybody hated Herman Lubinsky. If he messed with you, you were messed. At the same time, some of those people, many of them Newark's top singers and musicians, would never have been exposed on records if he didn't do what he did. Except for Lubinsky, all the hot little numbers, like Buddy Johnson's "Cherry", would have been lost. The man may have been hated, but he saved a lot of our history for us and for future generations.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy_Records#cite_note-6) Savoy's artistic directors included [Buck Ram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buck_Ram "Buck Ram"), [Teddy Reig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Reig "Teddy Reig"), [Ralph Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Bass "Ralph Bass") (1948–1952), [Fred Mendelsohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Mendelsohn "Fred Mendelsohn") (1953), and [Ozzie Cadena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzie_Cadena "Ozzie Cadena") (1954–1962). ## Discography _The following are 12" LPs and have the prefix MG._ | Cat | Artist | Album | | --- | --- | --- | | 12000 | [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker") | _Memorial 1_ | | 12001 | Charlie Parker | _Immortal Charlie Parker, The_ | | 12002 | [Erroll Garner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erroll_Garner "Erroll Garner") | _Penthouse Serenade_ | | 12003 | Erroll Garner | _Serenade to Laura_ | | 12004 | [Marian McPartland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marian_McPartland "Marian McPartland") | _At Storyville/At the Hickory House_ | | 12005 | Marian McPartland | _Lullaby of Birdland_ | | 12006 | [Kenny Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Clarke "Kenny Clarke") | _[Telefunken Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telefunken_Blues "Telefunken Blues")_ | | 12007 | Kenny Clarke and [Ernie Wilkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernie_Wilkins "Ernie Wilkins") | _[Kenny Clarke & Ernie Wilkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Clarke_&_Ernie_Wilkins "Kenny Clarke & Ernie Wilkins")_ | | 12008 | Erroll Garner/ [Billy Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Taylor "Billy Taylor") | _Back to Back_ | | 12009 | Charlie Parker | _Memorial 1_ | | 12010 | [J. Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability").
_Find sources:_ ["Jubilee Records"](https://www.google.com/search?as_eq=wikipedia&q=%22Jubilee+Records%22)– [news](https://www.google.com/search?tbm=nws&q=%22Jubilee+Records%22+-wikipedia&tbs=ar:1) **·** [newspapers](https://www.google.com/search?&q=%22Jubilee+Records%22&tbs=bkt:s&tbm=bks) **·** [books](https://www.google.com/search?tbs=bks:1&q=%22Jubilee+Records%22+-wikipedia) **·** [scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Jubilee+Records%22) **·** [JSTOR](https://www.jstor.org/action/doBasicSearch?Query=%22Jubilee+Records%22&acc=on&wc=on)_(May 2014)__([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ | Record label | Jubilee Records | | --- | | Parent company | [Warner Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Music_Group "Warner Music Group") | | Founded | 1946(1946) | | Founder | [Herb Abramson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Abramson "Herb Abramson") | | Defunct | 1971(1971) | | Genre | [Rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), [novelty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novelty_song "Novelty song") | | Country of origin | U.S. | | Location | [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") | **Jubilee Records** was an American [independent record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_record_label "Independent record label"), specializing in [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and novelty records. It was founded in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1946 by [Herb Abramson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Abramson "Herb Abramson"). His partner was [Jerry Blaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Blaine "Jerry Blaine"). Blaine bought Abramson's half of the company in 1947, when Abramson went on to co-found [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") with [Ahmet Ertegun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmet_Ertegun "Ahmet Ertegun").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-blaine-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-Inc.1959-2) The company name was Jay-Gee Recording Company, a subsidiary of the Cosnat Corporation. Cosnat was a wholesale record distributor. ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jubilee_Records&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] Jubilee was the first [independent record label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_record_label "Independent record label") to reach the white market with a black vocal group, when [the Orioles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Orioles "The Orioles")' recording of " [Crying in the Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crying_in_the_Chapel "Crying in the Chapel")" reached the Top Twenty on the [Pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music") chart in 1953.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-gillett-3) [The Four Tunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Four_Tunes "The Four Tunes") started recording for Jubilee in 1953. The biggest early hit for Jubilee was "Crying in the Chapel" by [the Orioles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Orioles "The Orioles"). A subsidiary label, [Josie Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josie_Records "Josie Records"), was formed in 1954 and issued more uptempo material. Hits on Josie included " [Speedoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speedoo "Speedoo")" by the [Cadillacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cadillacs "The Cadillacs") (number 3 R&B, number 17 pop) and " [Do You Want to Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_You_Want_to_Dance "Do You Want to Dance")" by [Bobby Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Freeman "Bobby Freeman") (number 2 R&B, number 5 pop). The biggest success was the million-seller " [Last Kiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Kiss "Last Kiss")", by J. Frank Wilson and the Cavaliers, which reached number 2 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") in 1964. In the late 1960s, [The Meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Meters "The Meters"), a group of New Orleans session musicians, released a series of R&B instrumental hits, including " [Cissy Strut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cissy_Strut "Cissy Strut")", which reached number 4 R&B and number 23 pop. The label's last [rock-and-roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll") hit was the [rhythm-and-blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") instrumental "Poor Boy"/"Wail!" by the Royaltones (number 17, 1957).[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-gillett-3) Of the label's novelty recordings, releases by the [blooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blooper "Blooper") compiler [Kermit Schaefer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kermit_Schaefer "Kermit Schaefer"), and the comedian [Rusty Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rusty_Warren "Rusty Warren") were successful. Jubilee/Josie also had a custom label, Gross Records, whose only artist was [Doug Clark and the Hot Nuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Clark_and_the_Hot_Nuts "Doug Clark and the Hot Nuts"); their material was so off-color that the Jubilee and Josie names appeared nowhere on their albums.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-4) In 1970, Jubilee/Josie, in financial difficulties, was sold to Viewlex, which owned [Buddah Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddah_Records "Buddah Records"), and Blaine left the company.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-5) The catalog was eventually taken over by [Roulette Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roulette_Records "Roulette Records").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-blaine-1) The label was declared bankrupt in 1971.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_Records#cite_note-6) In the late 1980s, Roulette was sold jointly to [Rhino Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhino_Records "Rhino Records") and [EMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMI "EMI"), and in the 1990s, Rhino was sold to [Time Warner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Warner "Time Warner"). The rights to the Jubilee Records archives in North America are now owned by Warner Music, with EMI holding the rights in the rest of the world until 2013. [Warner Music Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Music_Group "Warner Music Group") now has worldwide rights to the Roulette/Jubilee catalogue as a result of acquiring [Parlophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlophone "Parlophone") in 2013. ## Roster \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jubilee_Records&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Roster")\] This is a list of [recording artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_artists "Recording artists") who have had at least one [recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gramophone_record "Gramophone record") released on the Jubilee Records label. | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | [... middle omitted — see footer ...] | [Authority control databases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Authority_control "Help:Authority control")[![Edit this at Wikidata](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/8a/OOjs_UI_icon_edit-ltr-progressive.svg/20px-OOjs_UI_icon_edit-ltr-progressive.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q279035#identifiers "Edit this at Wikidata") | -
