(1970) | | _**Bitches Brew**_ is a studio album by the American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") trumpeter, composer, and bandleader [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"). It was recorded from August 19 to 21, 1969, at [Columbia's Studio B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Studio_Building "CBS Studio Building") in New York City and released on March 30, 1970, by [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). It marked Davis's continuing experimentation with electric instruments that he had featured on his previous record, the critically acclaimed _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ (1969). With these instruments, such as the [electric piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_piano "Electric piano") and [guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar"), Davis departed from traditional jazz rhythms in favor of loose, rock-influenced arrangements based on improvisation. The final tracks were edited and pieced together by producer [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero"). The album initially received a mixed critical and commercial response, but it gained momentum and became Davis's highest-charting album on the U.S. [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), peaking at No. 35. In [1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/13th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "13th Annual Grammy Awards"), it won the [Grammy Award for Best Large Jazz Ensemble Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Large_Jazz_Ensemble_Album "Grammy Award for Best Large Jazz Ensemble Album").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-7) In 1976, it became Davis's first album to be certified [Gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_(RIAA_certification) "Gold (RIAA certification)") by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA).[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-9) In subsequent years, _Bitches Brew_ gained recognition as one of jazz's greatest albums and a progenitor of the [jazz rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_rock "Jazz rock") genre, as well as a major influence on rock and '70s crossover musicians.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-Jurek-4) In 1998, Columbia released _[The Complete Bitches Brew Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_Bitches_Brew_Sessions "The Complete Bitches Brew Sessions")_,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-10) a four-disc box set that includes the original album and previously unreleased material. In 2003, the album was certified [Platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_(RIAA_certification) "Platinum (RIAA certification)") by the RIAA, reflecting shipments of one million copies in the United States. In 2025, the album was deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") and selected for preservation in the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-11) ## Background and recording [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Cbs-studio.jpg/330px-Cbs-studio.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cbs-studio.jpg) Current CBS Studio Building By 1969, Davis's core working band consisted of [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") on soprano saxophone, [Dave Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Holland_(bassist) "Dave Holland (bassist)") on bass, [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") on electric piano, and [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette") on drums.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990295-12) The group, minus DeJohnette, recorded _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ (1969), which also featured [Joe Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Zawinul "Joe Zawinul"), [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)"), [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)"), and [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"). The album marked the beginning of Davis's "electric period", incorporating instruments such as the [electric piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_piano "Electric piano"), guitar, and [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") styles.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990295-12) For his next studio album, Davis wished to explore his electronic and fusion style even further. While touring with his five-piece from the spring to August 1969, he introduced new pieces for his band to play, including early versions of what became "Miles Runs the Voodoo Down", "Sanctuary", and "Spanish Key".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-1999CD-13) At this point in his career Davis was influenced by contemporary rock and funk music, Zawinul's playing with [Cannonball Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley"), and the work of English composer [Paul Buckmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Buckmaster "Paul Buckmaster").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990298-14) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] hambers album)")_ ( [Joe Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Chambers "Joe Chambers"), 1978)

(1969) | | _**In a Silent Way**_ is a studio album by the American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") trumpeter, composer, and bandleader [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"), released on July 30, 1969, on [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). Produced by [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero"), the album was recorded in one session date on February 18, 1969, at [CBS 30th Street Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_30th_Street_Studio "CBS 30th Street Studio") in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"). Macero edited and arranged Davis's recordings from the session to produce the album. Marking the beginning of his ["electric" period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#1968%E2%80%931975:_The_electric_period "Miles Davis"), _In a Silent Way_ has been regarded by music writers as Davis's first [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") recording, following a stylistic shift toward the genre in his previous records and live performances. Upon its release, the album was met by controversy among music critics, particularly those of jazz and [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), who were divided in their reaction to its experimental musical structure and Davis's electric approach. It was nominated for the 1970 [Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Jazz_Instrumental_Album "Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album"). Since its initial reception, it has been regarded by fans and critics as one of Davis's greatest and most influential works. In 2001, Columbia Legacy and [Sony Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music_Entertainment "Sony Music Entertainment") released the three-disc box set _[The Complete In a Silent Way Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_In_a_Silent_Way_Sessions "The Complete In a Silent Way Sessions")_, which includes additional tracks.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-complete-4) ## Background and recording By January 1969, Davis' core working band had stabilised around [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") on soprano saxophone, [Dave Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Holland_(bassist) "Dave Holland (bassist)") on bass, [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") on electric piano, and [Jack DeJohnette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_DeJohnette "Jack DeJohnette") on drums.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990295-5) For his next studio album, Davis also brought in drummer [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)") and keyboardist [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), previously members of his [Second Great Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_great_quintet "Second great quintet").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990295-5) In the following month, the six were joined by Austrian keyboardist [Josef Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_Zawinul "Josef Zawinul")[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990296-6) and English guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)"), who had been in the United States for less than two weeks to join [The Tony Williams Lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime "The Tony Williams Lifetime") before Davis asked him to attend the recording session. McLaughlin had been a longtime fan of Davis, and spoke with Davis of his nervousness at the prospect of recording with his idol.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisTroupe1990296-6) Among the compositions by Zawinul that Davis took a liking to was "In a Silent Way", an atmospheric piece that was titled at the suggestion of [Nat Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nat_Adderley "Nat Adderley") while Zawinul was in the [Cannonball Adderley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannonball_Adderley "Cannonball Adderley") band. Adderley wished to use the piece for his band, but Zawinul turned him down, informing him that he had already promised it to Davis.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-tingen2001-7) Although Davis' live performances and recent albums _[Miles in the Sky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_in_the_Sky "Miles in the Sky")_ and _[Filles de Kilimanjaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filles_de_Kilimanjaro "Filles de Kilimanjaro")_ (both 1968) had indicated his stylistic shift towards [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") and increasing incorporation of electric instrumentation, _In a Silent Way_ marked a complete transition into the style, marking the beginning of his ["electric" period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#1968%E2%80%931975:_The_electric_period "Miles Davis").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Considine-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-Southall-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-O'Brien-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-11) It was also his first recording to be constructed largely by the editing and arrangement of Davis and producer [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero"),[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-O'Brien-10) whose editing techniques on _In a Silent Way_ were informed by classical [sonata form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonata_form "Sonata form").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-tingen2001-7) Both tracks on the album consist of three distinct parts that could be thought of as an [exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonata_form#Exposition "Sonata form"), [development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonata_form#Development "Sonata form"), and [recapitulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonata_form#Recapitulation "Sonata form"), with the first and third section of each track being the same piece.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way#cite_note-tingen2001-7) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] | Collaborative albums | - _[Super Released: 1974 | | | _**Head Hunters**_ is the twelfth [studio album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_album "Studio album") by American pianist, keyboardist and composer [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), released October 26, 1973, on [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). Recording sessions for the album took place in the evening at [Wally Heider Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wally_Heider_Studios "Wally Heider Studios") and [Different Fur Trading Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_Fur "Different Fur") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"). Hancock is featured with woodwind player [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin") from his previous "Mwandishi" sextet and three new collaborators – bassist [Paul Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Jackson_(bassist) "Paul Jackson (bassist)"), percussionist [Bill Summers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Summers_(musician) "Bill Summers (musician)"), and drummer [Harvey Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Mason "Harvey Mason"). The latter group of collaborators, which would go on to be known as [the Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters"), also played on Hancock's subsequent studio album _[Thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_(album) "Thrust (album)")_ (1974). All of the musicians (with the exception of Mason) play multiple instruments on the album. The album was a commercial and artistic breakthrough for Hancock, crossing over to [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") audiences and bringing [jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk "Jazz-funk") and [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") to mainstream attention, peaking at number 13 on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"). Today the album is regarded as a landmark of fusion and has influenced artists in numerous other genres. In 2008, the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") inducted it into the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry") for being "culturally, historically or aesthetically important".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_Hunters#cite_note-3) ## Background and recording _Head Hunters_ followed three experimental albums by Hancock's "Mwandishi" sextet: _[Mwandishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwandishi "Mwandishi")_, _[Crossings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossings_(Herbie_Hancock_album) "Crossings (Herbie Hancock album)")_, and _[Sextant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextant_(album) "Sextant (album)")_, released between 1971 and 1973. He later reflected on moving away from this style: > I began to feel that I had been spending so much time exploring the upper atmosphere of music and the more ethereal kind of far-out spacey stuff. Now there was this need to take some more of the earth and to feel a little more tethered; a connection to the earth. ... I was beginning to feel that we (the sextet) were playing this heavy kind of music, and I was tired of everything being heavy. I wanted to play something lighter. —Hancock's sleeve notes: 1997 CD reissue For the new album, Hancock assembled a new band, [the Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters"), of whom only woodwind player [Bennie Maupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennie_Maupin "Bennie Maupin") had been a member of the "Mwandishi" sextet. Hancock handled all synthesizer parts himself, having shared these duties with [Patrick Gleeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Gleeson "Patrick Gleeson") on _Crossings_ and _Sextant,_ and decided against the use of guitar altogether in favor of the Hohner [Clavinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavinet "Clavinet"), one of the defining sounds on the album. The new band featured a tight [rhythm section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_section "Rhythm section") composed of [Paul Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Jackson_(bassist) "Paul Jackson (bassist)") (bass guitar) and [Harvey Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Mason "Harvey Mason") (drums), creating a relaxed [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") sensibility that gave it an appeal to a wider audience. [Andrew White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_White_(saxophonist) "Andrew White (saxophonist)") | **Weather Report** was an American [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") band active from 1970 to 1986. The band was founded in 1970 by Austrian keyboardist [Joe Zawinul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Zawinul "Joe Zawinul"), American saxophonist [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), Czech bassist [Miroslav Vitouš](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miroslav_Vitou%C5%A1 "Miroslav Vitouš"), American drummer [Alphonse Mouzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Mouzon "Alphonse Mouzon") and American percussionists [Don Alias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Alias "Don Alias") and Barbara Burton. The band was initially co-led by Zawinul and Shorter but as the 1970s progressed, Zawinul became the primary composer and creative director of the group. Other prominent members throughout the band's history included bassists [Jaco Pastorius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaco_Pastorius "Jaco Pastorius"), [Alphonso Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonso_Johnson "Alphonso Johnson") and [Victor Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Bailey_(musician) "Victor Bailey (musician)"), drummers [Chester Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester_Thompson "Chester Thompson"), [Peter Erskine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Erskine "Peter Erskine") and [Omar Hakim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omar_Hakim "Omar Hakim"), and percussionists [Airto Moreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airto_Moreira "Airto Moreira") and [Alex Acuña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Acu%C3%B1a "Alex Acuña"). A quintet of Zawinul and Shorter plus a bassist, a drummer, and a percussionist was the standard formation for Weather Report. The band started as a free improvising group with avant-garde and experimental electronic leanings (pioneered by Zawinul); when Vitouš left Weather Report (due mostly to creative disagreements), Zawinul increasingly steered the band towards a funky, edgy sound incorporating elements of [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and native musics from around the world. Zawinul used the latest developments in synthesizer technology, and he took advantage of a large variety of sounds and tone colors to make the band stand out. During the first half of their career, Weather Report were seen as one of the defining acts in modern jazz, winning the [DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat") "best album award" five times in a row. Alongside bands such as [Mahavishnu Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra "Mahavishnu Orchestra"), [Return to Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever "Return to Forever"), and [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock")'s [Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters") (all with members inspired by and partially responsible for the fusion-era work of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")), Weather Report is widely considered one of the defining bands of the [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") genre. ## Musical style Over their 16-year career, Weather Report explored various types of music, predominantly centered on jazz (initially the " [free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz")" variety), but also incorporating elements of [art music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_music "Art music"), [ethnic music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"), [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"). While their work was categorized as "jazz fusion", the band members generally distanced themselves from that term. From the start, Weather Report took the unusual approach of abandoning the traditional "soloist/accompaniment" demarcation of straight-ahead jazz and featured opportunities for continuous improvisation by every member of the band. That position remained consistent throughout the life of the band. From the point where [Alphonso Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonso_Johnson "Alphonso Johnson") joined the band, individual solos became more prominent in concert, but were never allowed to overwhelm the collective approach. Initially, the band's music featured an improvisational method (similar to [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_-period),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report#cite_note-Larkin-1) but eventually that shifted to a more groove-oriented approach and catchier compositions (as epitomized by their 1977 hit single ["Birdland"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birdland_(composition) "Birdland (composition)")). [Jean-Luc Ponty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Ponty "Jean-Luc Ponty") | | | | Website | [return2forever.com](http://return2forever.com/) | **Return to Forever** was an American [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") band that was founded by pianist [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") in 1972.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_to_Forever#cite_note-Larkin-2) The band has had many members, with the only consistent bandmate of Corea's being bassist [Stanley Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Clarke "Stanley Clarke"). Along with [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report"), [The Headhunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Headhunters "The Headhunters"), and [Mahavishnu Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra "Mahavishnu Orchestra"), Return to Forever is often cited as one of the core groups of the jazz-fusion movement of the 1970s. Several musicians, including Clarke, [Flora Purim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flora_Purim "Flora Purim"), [Airto Moreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airto_Moreira "Airto Moreira") and [Al Di Meola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Di_Meola "Al Di Meola"), came to prominence through their performances on Return to Forever albums. After playing on [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s jazz-fusion albums _[In a Silent Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_a_Silent_Way "In a Silent Way")_ (1969) and _[Bitches Brew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitches_Brew "Bitches Brew")_ (1970), Corea formed an [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") band called [Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_(American_band) "Circle (American band)") with [Dave Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Holland_(bassist) "Dave Holland (bassist)"), [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton") and [Barry Altschul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Altschul "Barry Altschul"). In 1972, after converting to [Scientology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientology "Scientology"), Corea decided he wanted to communicate better with his audience. This meant performing a more accessible style of music than avant-garde jazz. Return to Forever first disbanded in 1977 after five years and seven studio albums. The band never released another studio album, but occasionally reunited for live performances until Corea's death in 2021. ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Return_to_Forever&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] ### First group (1972–1973) \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Return_to_Forever&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: First group (1972–1973)")\] [... middle omitted — see footer ...] - [Jim Beard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Beard "Jim Beard") | The **Mahavishnu Orchestra** was a [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") band formed in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") in 1971, led by English guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-Larkin-1) The group underwent several line-up changes throughout its history across its two periods of activity, from 1971 to 1976 and from 1984 to 1987.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-2) With its first line-up consisting of McLaughlin, drummer [Billy Cobham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Cobham "Billy Cobham"), keyboardist [Jan Hammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Hammer "Jan Hammer"), violinist [Jerry Goodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Goodman "Jerry Goodman") and bassist [Rick Laird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Laird "Rick Laird"), the band received acclaim for its complex, intense music consisting of a blend of [Indian classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_classical_music "Indian classical music"), [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), and [psychedelic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock "Psychedelic rock") as well as its dynamic live performances between 1971 and 1973.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-harvardcrimson-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-newyorktimes1-4) Many members of the band have gone on to acclaimed careers of their own in the jazz and jazz-fusion genres. ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mahavishnu_Orchestra&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] ### 1971–1974: First incarnation \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mahavishnu_Orchestra&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: 1971–1974: First incarnation")\] By mid-1971, McLaughlin had been a member of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")' band and [Tony Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Williams_(drummer) "Tony Williams (drummer)")' Lifetime, and released three solo albums. He then set about forming his own [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") group, the first line-up of which featured Panamanian drummer Cobham, Irish bassist Laird, Czech keyboardist Hammer and American violinist Goodman.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-CD11-73-5) Cobham and Goodman had played on McLaughlin's third solo album _[My Goal's Beyond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Goal's_Beyond "My Goal's Beyond")_ (1971). McLaughlin's first choice for violinist was Frenchman [Jean-Luc Ponty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Luc_Ponty "Jean-Luc Ponty"), but he was unable to join due to immigration problems. After listening to various albums he hired Goodman, formerly of [the Flock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Flock_(band) "The Flock (band)"). Though American bassist [Tony Levin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Levin "Tony Levin") was the first person McLaughlin wanted,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-7) Laird had known McLaughlin for several years and accepted the invitation. Hammer was found through a mutual friendship with [Miroslav Vitouš](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miroslav_Vitou%C5%A1 "Miroslav Vitouš") of the jazz fusion group [Weather Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Report "Weather Report").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-CD11-73-5) The group's name originates from Indian spiritual leader and guru [Sri Chinmoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Chinmoy "Sri Chinmoy"), of whom McLaughlin had become a follower, who gave him the name Mahavishnu, "Maha" meaning "great" in [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") and "vishnu" after the Hindu deity [Vishnu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vishnu "Vishnu").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-8) With the line-up secured, the five met in New York City in July 1971 and rehearsed for one week. They adopted an instrumental fusion sound characterised by electric rock, funk, complex [time signatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_signatures "Time signatures"), and arrangements influenced by McLaughlin's interest in [Indian classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_classical_music "Indian classical music"). Their debut gigs followed at the [Gaslight at the Au Go Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cafe_Au_Go_Go "Cafe Au Go Go") as the opening act for bluesman [John Lee Hooker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lee_Hooker "John Lee Hooker").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-9) McLaughlin recalled: "The first set was shaky but the second set just took off and every night it was great. They wanted to hold us over and a few days after the second week ... we went into the studio".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahavishnu_Orchestra#cite_note-crawdaddy1973-10) McLaughlin secured a record deal with [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), giving the green light to record an album. - (see [Personnel section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#Personnel) for others) | | | | Website | [santana.com](http://santana.com/) | **Santana** is an American [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_Music "Rock Music") band formed in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), California in 1966 by Mexican-American guitarist [Carlos Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Santana "Carlos Santana").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-10) The band has had various recording and performing line-ups in its history, with Santana being the only consistent member. After signing with [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), the band's appearance at the [Woodstock Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodstock_Festival "Woodstock Festival") in 1969 increased their profile and they went on to record the critically acclaimed and commercially successful albums _[Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(1969_album) "Santana (1969 album)")_ (1969), _[Abraxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraxas_(album) "Abraxas (album)")_ (1970) and _[Santana III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(1971_album) "Santana (1971 album)")_ (1971). These were recorded by the group's "classic" line-up, comprising organist and lead vocalist [Gregg Rolie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregg_Rolie "Gregg Rolie"), percussionists [José "Chepito" Areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Areas "José Areas") and [Michael Carabello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Carabello "Michael Carabello"), drummer [Michael Shrieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Shrieve "Michael Shrieve") and bassist [David Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Brown_(American_musician) "David Brown (American musician)"). Hit songs of this period include " [Evil Ways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evil_Ways_(Santana_song) "Evil Ways (Santana song)")" (1970), " [Black Magic Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Magic_Woman "Black Magic Woman")" (1970), " [Oye Como Va](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oye_Como_Va "Oye Como Va")" (1971) and the instrumental " [Samba Pa Ti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba_Pa_Ti_(instrumental) "Samba Pa Ti (instrumental)")" (1970). Following a change in line-up and musical direction in 1972, the band experimented with elements of [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") on _[Caravanserai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravanserai_(album) "Caravanserai (album)")_ (1972), _[Welcome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welcome_(Santana_album) "Welcome (Santana album)")_ (1973) and _[Borboletta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borboletta "Borboletta")_ (1974). The band reached a new peak of critical and commercial success with their eighteenth album, _[Supernatural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_(Santana_album) "Supernatural (Santana album)")_ (1999), which included the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100")-number one singles " [Smooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_(Santana_song) "Smooth (Santana song)")" (featuring [Rob Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Thomas_(musician) "Rob Thomas (musician)")) and " [Maria Maria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Maria "Maria Maria")" (featuring [The Product G&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Product_G&B "The Product G&B")). The album peaked atop the charts in eleven countries and sold 12million copies domestically. It won eight [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards") at the [42nd Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_Annual_Grammy_Awards "42nd Annual Grammy Awards"), a record tied with [Michael Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jackson "Michael Jackson"), and three [Latin Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Grammy_Awards "Latin Grammy Awards").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-11) In 2014, the "classic" line-up—with the exception of Brown, who died in 2000, and Areas, who was not invited to participate[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_(band)#cite_note-12)—reunited for the _[Santana IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santana_IV "Santana IV")_ album (2016) and tour. (1966) | | _**Ascension**_ is a studio album by the [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") composer and musician [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"). It was released through [Impulse! Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records") in February 1966. It is considered a watershed in Coltrane's work, with the albums recorded before it being more conventional in structure and the albums recorded after it being looser, [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") inspired works. In addition, it signaled Coltrane's interest in moving away from the quartet format. [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called it "the single recording that placed John Coltrane firmly into the avant-garde".[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-allmusic-2) It was recorded at the [Van Gelder Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Gelder_Studio "Van Gelder Studio") in June 1965. ## Background At the time of the _Ascension_ recording session, Coltrane was one of the world's most successful jazz artists in both the artistic and commercial sense. His best-selling album _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-3) was nominated for a Grammy Award,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-4) and was voted "album of the year" by both _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ and _[Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Magazine "Jazz Magazine")_ magazines.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-porter262-5) In addition, Coltrane was elected to DownBeat's Hall of Fame, putting him in the company of [Coleman Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coleman_Hawkins "Coleman Hawkins") and [Lester Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Young "Lester Young").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-porter262-5) At the same time, in the months since _A Love Supreme_ was recorded, Coltrane's music had become increasingly turbulent, moving further in the direction of free jazz.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-6) Coltrane had befriended saxophonist [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"), and was heavily influenced by his music;[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-7) meanwhile, he had also become somewhat of a father figure for a number of younger avant-garde players, some of whom would appear on _Ascension_.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-8) According to writer Bernard Gendron, "At the height of his career, riding on the momentum of the critical and popular triumph of _A Love Supreme_, Coltrane was the modern jazz star of the 1960s, with a large following of serious jazz fans and great respect from his musician peers. He was in an ideal position to bring into the orbit of the avant-garde fans and musicians who had previously hesitated, been puzzled or mildly hostile."[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-9) ## Additional musicians The musicians that Coltrane chose to supplement the members of the classic quartet were a mix of players ranging from established to relatively unknown, all of whom were younger than Coltrane, and many of whom had played with Coltrane in the years preceding the recording of _Ascension._[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-10) Trumpeter [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard") and bassist [Art Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Davis_(bassist) "Art Davis (bassist)") were well-known and well-recorded by that point, and both had recorded with Coltrane on _[Africa/Brass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa/Brass "Africa/Brass")_ and _[Olé Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ol%C3%A9_Coltrane "Olé Coltrane")_. (Davis also appeared on _[The John Coltrane Quartet Plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_John_Coltrane_Quartet_Plays "The John Coltrane Quartet Plays")_, recorded earlier in 1965.) Saxophonist [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp") recorded his first [Impulse!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records") album, _[Four for Trane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_for_Trane "Four for Trane")_, in 1964 after Coltrane recommended him to producer [Bob Thiele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Thiele "Bob Thiele"),[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-house-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-giddins_first_century-12) and went on to release over a dozen albums on the label. Shepp, along with Art Davis, also appeared on an alternate take of the "Acknowledgement" section of _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_, which was released more than thirty years after the appearance of the original recording.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-13)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_(John_Coltrane_album)#cite_note-14) Shortly after the recording of _Ascension_, Shepp appeared on _[New Thing at Newport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Thing_at_Newport "New Thing at Newport")_, a split LP with Coltrane's quartet appearing on side one and Shepp's quartet on side two. (1965) | | _**A Love Supreme**_ is an album by the American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") saxophonist and composer [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"). It was recorded in one session on December 9, 1964, at [Van Gelder Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Gelder_Studio "Van Gelder Studio") in [Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Englewood_Cliffs,_New_Jersey "Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey"), with a quartet featuring pianist [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner"), bassist [Jimmy Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Garrison "Jimmy Garrison"), and drummer [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones"). _A Love Supreme_ was released by [Impulse! Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse!_Records "Impulse! Records") in January 1965. Referred to as the saxophonist's "definitive tone poem", it ranks among Coltrane's best-selling albums and is widely considered one of the greatest masterpieces in the history of jazz and one of the greatest albums ever made.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-:0-2) It was nominated for the 1966 [Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Jazz_Instrumental_Album "Grammy Award for Best Jazz Instrumental Album"). ## Composition _A Love Supreme_ is a [through-composed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Through-composed_music "Through-composed music")[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-xgau-3) [suite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suite_(music) "Suite (music)")[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-nyt-4) in four parts: "Acknowledgement" (which includes the oral chant that gives the album its name), "Resolution", "Pursuance", and "Psalm". Coltrane plays [tenor saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_saxophone "Tenor saxophone") on all parts. One critic has written that the album was intended to represent a struggle for purity, an expression of gratitude, and an acknowledgement that the musician's talent comes from a higher power.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-kahn-5) The album's improvisational and spiritual intensity has led some to liken it to [glossolalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaking_in_tongues "Speaking in tongues"), or speaking in tongues, as it conveys a profound sense of ecstatic devotion.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-6) This sacred quality has led it to become the "central text" of the [Saint John Coltrane African Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_John_Coltrane_African_Orthodox_Church "Saint John Coltrane African Orthodox Church") in San Francisco.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-7) [Coltrane's home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane_Home "John Coltrane Home") in [Dix Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dix_Hills,_New_York "Dix Hills, New York"), Long Island, may have inspired the album.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-kahn-5) Another influence may have been [Ahmadiyya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmadiyya "Ahmadiyya") Islam.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-HammerSafi2013-8) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/A_Love_Supreme.jpg/500px-A_Love_Supreme.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_Love_Supreme.jpg) Coltrane's handwritten notes for _A Love Supreme_ According to assistant music editor at _[Time Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Out_(magazine) "Time Out (magazine)")_ John Lewis, the album "pulls off the rare trick of being utterly uncompromising yet completely accessible."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-:0-2) [![Elvin Jones in a black suit performing behind a drum kit](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Elvin_Jones_3.jpg/500px-Elvin_Jones_3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elvin_Jones_3.jpg) [Elvin Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvin_Jones "Elvin Jones") (pictured in 1976) The album begins with the bang of a gong ( [tam-tam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tam-tam "Tam-tam")) and cymbal washes on the first track, "Acknowledgement". [Jimmy Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Garrison "Jimmy Garrison") enters on double bass with the four-note motif that lays the foundation of the movement. Coltrane begins a solo. He plays variations on the motif until he repeats the four notes thirty-six times. The motif then becomes the vocal chant "a love supreme", sung by Coltrane accompanying himself through overdubs nineteen times.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-9) According to _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_, this movement's four-note theme is "the humble foundation of the suite".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-RS500-10) ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg/120px-Gnome-mime-audio-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) ["Part 1: Acknowledgement"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:John_Coltrane_-_Acknowledgement.ogg "File:John Coltrane - Acknowledgement.ogg") The first 30 seconds of "Part 1: Acknowledgement", the first track on _A Love Supreme_ * * * _Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._ In the fourth and final movement, "Psalm", Coltrane performs what he calls a "musical narration". [Lewis Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Porter "Lewis Porter") calls it a "wordless recitation".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-11) The devotional is included in the [liner notes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liner_notes "Liner notes"). Coltrane "plays" the words of the poem on saxophone but doesn't speak them. Some scholars have suggested that this performance is an homage to the [sermons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sermon "Sermon") of [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") preachers.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme#cite_note-12) The poem (and, in his own way, Coltrane's solo) ends with the cry, "Elation. - Elliot Ngubone | | | | Website | [www.artensembleofchicago.com](http://www.artensembleofchicago.com/) | The **Art Ensemble of Chicago** is an [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") group that grew out of the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians ( [AACM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians "Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians")) in the late 1960s.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-RCJE-1) The ensemble integrates many jazz styles and plays many instruments, including "little instruments": bells, bicycle horns, birthday party noisemakers, wind chimes, and various forms of percussion. The musicians would wear costumes and face paint while performing. These characteristics combined to make the ensemble's performances both aural and visual. While playing in Europe in 1969, five hundred instruments were used.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-2) ## History Members of what was to become the Art Ensemble performed together under various band names in the mid-sixties, as members of the [Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians "Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians") (AACM). They performed on the 1966 album _[Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_(Roscoe_Mitchell_album) "Sound (Roscoe Mitchell album)"),_ as the [Roscoe Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscoe_Mitchell "Roscoe Mitchell") Sextet. The Sextet included saxophonist Roscoe Mitchell, trumpeter [Lester Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bowie "Lester Bowie"), and bassist [Malachi Favors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malachi_Favors "Malachi Favors"). For the next year, they played as the Roscoe Mitchell Art Ensemble. In 1967, they were joined by fellow AACM members [Joseph Jarman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Jarman "Joseph Jarman") (saxophone) and [Phillip Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillip_Wilson_(drummer) "Phillip Wilson (drummer)") (drums) and recorded for [Nessa Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nessa_Records "Nessa Records"). All of the musicians were multi-instrumentalists. Jarman and Mitchell's primary instruments were [alto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alto_saxophone "Alto saxophone") and [tenor saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_saxophone "Tenor saxophone"), respectively. Additionally, they both played other saxophones ranging from the small [sopranino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sopranino_saxophone "Sopranino saxophone") to the large [bass saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_saxophone "Bass saxophone"), as well as the flute and clarinet. In addition to trumpet, Bowie played [flugelhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flugelhorn "Flugelhorn"), [cornet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornet "Cornet"), [shofar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shofar "Shofar"), and [conch shells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conch_shell "Conch shell"). Favors added touches of banjo and bass guitar. Most of them dabbled in piano, [synthesizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer"), and other keyboards, and they all played percussion instruments. They were known for wearing costumes and makeup on stage. Member [Joseph Jarman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Jarman "Joseph Jarman") described part of their style: > So what we were doing with that face painting was representing everyone throughout the universe, and that was expressed in the music as well. That's why the music was so interesting. It wasn't limited to Western instruments, African instruments, or Asian instruments, or South American instruments, or anybody's instruments.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-3) In 1967, Wilson left the group to join [Paul Butterfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Butterfield "Paul Butterfield")'s band, and for a period the group was a quartet without a full-time drummer. [Jarman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarman "Jarman") and [Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscoe_Mitchell "Roscoe Mitchell") served as artistic directors at the [cooperative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperative "Cooperative") summer camp [Circle Pines Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_Pines_Center?action=edit&redlink=1 "Circle Pines Center") in [Delton, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delton,_Michigan "Delton, Michigan"), in August 1968, during the same week that the Democratic Convention was in Chicago. After a farewell concert at the Unitarian Church in [Evanston, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evanston,_Illinois "Evanston, Illinois"), in fall, 1968, the remaining group traveled to Paris.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-Wilmer,_Valerie_1977_122%E2%80%93123-4) In Paris, the ensemble was based at the Théâtre du Vieux Colombier.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-Jost,_Ekkehard_1975_167-5)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-Wilmer,_Valerie_1977_122%E2%80%93123-4) In France, they became known as the Art Ensemble of Chicago. The impetus for the name change came from a French promoter who added "of Chicago" to their name for descriptive purposes. The new name stuck because band members felt that it better reflected the cooperative nature of the group. In Paris, the ensemble was based at the Théâtre du Vieux Colombier [\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago#cite_note-Jost,_Ekkehard_1975_167-5) and they recorded for the [Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_Records_(jazz_label) "Freedom Records (jazz label)") and [BYG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BYG_Actuel "BYG Actuel") labels. They also recorded _[Comme à la radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comme_%C3%A0_la_radio "Comme à la radio")_ with [Brigitte Fontaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigitte_Fontaine "Brigitte Fontaine") and [Areski Belkacem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areski_Belkacem "Areski Belkacem") but without a drummer until percussionist [Don Moye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Moye "Don Moye") became a member of the group in 1970. During that year, they recorded the albums _[Art Ensemble of Chicago with Fontella Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago_with_Fontella_Bass "Art Ensemble of Chicago with Fontella Bass")_ and _[Les Stances a Sophie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Stances_a_Sophie "Les Stances a Sophie")_ with singer [Fontella Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontella_Bass "Fontella Bass"), who was Lester Bowie's wife. The latter was the soundtrack to the French movie of the same title. - [Universal Classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Group "Universal Music Group") | | | | Website | [keith-jarrett.de/en](https://keith-jarrett.de/en) | Musical artist **Keith Jarrett** (born May 8, 1945) is an American pianist and [composer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composer "Composer").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Larkin-1) Jarrett started his career with [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey") and later moved on to play with [Charles Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lloyd_(jazz_musician) "Charles Lloyd (jazz musician)") and [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"). Since the early 1970s, he has also been a group leader and solo performer in [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion"), and [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"). His improvisations draw from the traditions of jazz and other genres, including Western classical music, [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music"), [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"), and ethnic [folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"). His album _[The Köln Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_K%C3%B6ln_Concert "The Köln Concert")_, released in 1975, is the best-selling piano recording in history.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-3) In 2008, he was inducted into the _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ Jazz Hall of Fame in the magazine's 73rd Annual Readers' Poll.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-4) In 2003, Jarrett received the [Polar Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_Music_Prize "Polar Music Prize") and was the first recipient to be recognized with the prizes for both contemporary and classical music.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-5) In 2004, he received the [Léonie Sonning Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9onie_Sonning_Music_Prize "Léonie Sonning Music Prize"). In February 2018, Jarrett suffered a [stroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke "Stroke") and has been unable to perform since. A second stroke in May 2018 left him partially paralyzed and unable to play with his left hand.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-:0-6) ## Early life and education \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")\] Jarrett was born on May 8, 1945, in [Allentown, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allentown,_Pennsylvania "Allentown, Pennsylvania"),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-Larkin-1) to a mother of [Slovenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovenes "Slovenes") descent. Jarrett's grandmother was born in [Segovci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Segovci "Segovci"), near [Apače](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apa%C4%8De "Apače") in [Slovenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovenia "Slovenia").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-7) Jarrett's father was of mostly [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germans "Germans") descent.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-8) He grew up in suburban Allentown with significant early exposure to music.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-9) Jarrett possesses [absolute pitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_pitch "Absolute pitch") and displayed prodigious musical talents as a young child. He began piano lessons before his third birthday. At age five, he appeared on a television talent program hosted by swing bandleader [Paul Whiteman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Whiteman "Paul Whiteman").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-10) He performed in his first formal piano recital at the age of seven, playing works by composers such as [Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach"), [Beethoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_van_Beethoven "Ludwig van Beethoven"), [Mozart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart "Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart"), and [Saint-Saëns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Saint-Sa%C3%ABns "Camille Saint-Saëns"), and ending with two of his own compositions.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-11) Encouraged by his mother, he took classical piano lessons with a series of teachers, including [Eleanor Sokoloff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleanor_Sokoloff "Eleanor Sokoloff") of the [Curtis Institute of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtis_Institute_of_Music "Curtis Institute of Music") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"). Jarrett attended [Emmaus High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmaus_High_School "Emmaus High School") in [Emmaus, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmaus,_Pennsylvania "Emmaus, Pennsylvania"), where he learned [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") and became proficient in it. He developed a strong interest in [contemporary jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") and was inspired by a [Dave Brubeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Brubeck "Dave Brubeck") performance he attended in [New Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Hope,_Pennsylvania "New Hope, Pennsylvania").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-12) He was invited to study classical composition in Paris with [Nadia Boulanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadia_Boulanger "Nadia Boulanger"), but he was already leaning toward jazz and turned it down.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Jarrett#cite_note-13) After his graduation from Emmaus High School in 1963, Jarrett moved to [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") to attend [Berklee College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berklee_College_of_Music "Berklee College of Music") and play [cocktail piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_bar "Piano bar") in local Boston clubs. ## Career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Career")\] ### The Jazz Messengers \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Keith_Jarrett&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: The Jazz Messengers")\] Main article: [The Jazz Messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Messengers "The Jazz Messengers") [... middle omitted — see footer ...] - - gamelan | Musical artist **Donald Eugene Cherry** (November 18, 1936 – October 19, 1995)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-1) was an American jazz trumpeter, bandleader, and multi-instrumentalist. Beginning in the late 1950s, he had a long tenure performing in the bands of saxophonist [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), including on the pioneering [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") albums _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_ (1959) and _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_ (1961). Cherry also collaborated separately with musicians including [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra"), [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), the [New York Contemporary Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Contemporary_Five "New York Contemporary Five"), and [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"). Cherry released his debut album as bandleader, _[Complete Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Communion "Complete Communion")_, in 1966. In the 1970s, he became a pioneer in [world fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music"), with his work drawing on African, Middle Eastern, and [Hindustani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindustani_classical_music "Hindustani classical music") music, as heard on the 1975 release _[Brown Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Rice_(album) "Brown Rice (album)")_. He was a member of the [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_Records "ECM Records") group [Codona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codona "Codona"), along with percussionist [Naná Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nan%C3%A1_Vasconcelos "Naná Vasconcelos") and sitar and tabla player [Collin Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Walcott "Collin Walcott").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-2) Chris Kelsey of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called Cherry "one of the most influential jazz musicians of the late 20th century."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-3) ## Early life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life")\] Cherry was born in [Oklahoma City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City "Oklahoma City"), [Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma "Oklahoma"), to a mother of [Choctaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choctaw "Choctaw") descent and an [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") father.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-4) His mother and grandmother played piano and his father played trumpet.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-atc1995-5) His father owned Oklahoma City's Cherry Blossom Club, which hosted performances by jazz musicians [Charlie Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Christian "Charlie Christian") and [Fletcher Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fletcher_Henderson "Fletcher Henderson").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-biojazz-6) In 1940, Cherry moved with his family to the [Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts,_Los_Angeles "Watts, Los Angeles") neighborhood of [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), where his father tended bar at the Plantation Club on [Central Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Avenue_(Los_Angeles) "Central Avenue (Los Angeles)"), at the time the center of a vibrant jazz scene.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-biojazz-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-carr-8) Cherry recalled skipping school at [Fremont High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Fremont_High_School "John C. Fremont High School") in order to play with the [swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_music "Swing music") band at [Jefferson High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_High_School_(Los_Angeles) "Jefferson High School (Los Angeles)").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) This resulted in his transfer to Jacob Riis High School, a [reform school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_school "Reform school"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-cadence-7) where he met drummer [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-voce1995-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)#cite_note-crouch-10) ## Career \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Don_Cherry_(trumpeter)&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Career")\] [... middle omitted — see footer ...] - The two main categories are [Afro-Cuban jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Cuban_jazz "Afro-Cuban jazz"), rhythmically based on Cuban popular dance music, with a rhythm section employing [ostinato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato "Ostinato") patterns or a [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)"), and Afro-Brazilian jazz, which includes [samba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samba "Samba") and [bossa nova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bossa_nova "Bossa nova"). ## Afro-Cuban jazz \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Afro-Cuban jazz")\] Main article: [Afro-Cuban jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Cuban_jazz "Afro-Cuban jazz") ### "Spanish tinge"—The Cuban influence in early jazz and proto-Latin jazz \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: \"Spanish tinge\"—The Cuban influence in early jazz and proto-Latin jazz")\] [African American music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American_music "African American music") began incorporating [Afro-Cuban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Cuban "Afro-Cuban") musical motifs in the 19th century, when the [habanera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habanera_(music) "Habanera (music)") (Cuban [contradanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contradanza "Contradanza")) gained international popularity. The habanera was the first written music to be rhythmically based on an African motif. The _habanera rhythm_ (also known as _congo_,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-1) _tango-congo_,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-2) or _[tango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tango_(music) "Tango (music)")_[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-3)) can be thought of as a combination of [tresillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tresillo_(rhythm) "Tresillo (rhythm)") and the [backbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music)#Backbeat "Beat (music)"). [Wynton Marsalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Marsalis "Wynton Marsalis") considers [tresillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tresillo_(rhythm) "Tresillo (rhythm)") to be the New Orleans "clave," although technically, the pattern is only half a [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-4) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Tresillo_divisive.png/250px-Tresillo_divisive.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tresillo_divisive.png) Tresillo [Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/8/8c/Tresillo_divisive.mid/Tresillo_divisive.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tresillo_divisive.mid "File:Tresillo divisive.mid")[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f2/Basic_habanera_rhythm%2C_Orovio_1981_237.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Basic_habanera_rhythm,_Orovio_1981_237.png) Habanera rhythm[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-5) " [St. Louis Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Blues_(song) "St. Louis Blues (song)")" (1914) by [W. C. Handy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._C._Handy "W. C. Handy") has a habanera-tresillo bass line. Handy noted a reaction to the habanera rhythm included in Will H. Tyler's "Maori": "I observed that there was a sudden, proud and graceful reaction to the rhythm...White dancers, as I had observed them, took the number in stride. I began to suspect that there was something Negroid in that beat." After noting a similar reaction to the same rhythm in "La Paloma", Handy included this rhythm in his "St. Louis Blues", the instrumental copy of "Memphis Blues", the chorus of "Beale Street Blues", and other compositions.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-autogenerated2-6) [Jelly Roll Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelly_Roll_Morton "Jelly Roll Morton") considered the tresillo-habanera (which he called the [Spanish tinge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_tinge "Spanish tinge")) to be an essential ingredient of jazz.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-7) The habanera rhythm can be heard in his left hand on songs like "The Crave" (1910, recorded 1938). > Now in one of my earliest tunes, "New Orleans Blues," you can notice the Spanish tinge. In fact, if you can't manage to put tinges of Spanish in your tunes, you will never be able to get the right seasoning, I call it, for jazz—Morton (1938: Library of Congress Recording).[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-8) [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/35/MortonBricktopRowCropMortonFace.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MortonBricktopRowCropMortonFace.jpg) Jelly Roll Morton Although the exact origins of jazz syncopation may never be known, there is evidence that the habanera-tresillo was there at its conception. [Buddy Bolden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_Bolden "Buddy Bolden"), the first _known_ jazz musician, is credited with creating the _big four_, a habanera-based pattern. The big four (below) was the first syncopated bass drum pattern to deviate from the standard on-the-beat march.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-9) As the example below shows, the second half of the big four pattern is the habanera rhythm. [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Big_four_Buddy_Bolden.png/330px-Big_four_Buddy_Bolden.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Big_four_Buddy_Bolden.png) Buddy Bolden's "big four" pattern > It is probably safe to say that by and large the simpler African rhythmic patterns survived in jazz... because they could be adapted more readily to European rhythmic conceptions. Some survived, others were discarded as the Europeanization progressed. It may also account for the fact that patterns such as \[tresillo have\] . . . remained one of the most useful and common syncopated patterns in jazz—Schuller (1968).[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-10) The Cuban influence is evident in many pre-1940s jazz tunes, but rhythmically, they are all based on single-celled motifs such as [tresillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tresillo_(rhythm) "Tresillo (rhythm)"), and not do not contain an overt two-celled, [clave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clave_(rhythm) "Clave (rhythm)")-based structure. " [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(1937_song) "Caravan (1937 song)")", written by [Juan Tizol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Tizol "Juan Tizol") and [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington") and first performed in 1936, is an early proto-Latin jazz composition. [Mongo Santamaría](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongo_Santamar%C3%ADa "Mongo Santamaría") recorded ever green "Watermelon Man" in 1962. [Hank Mobley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hank_Mobley "Hank Mobley"), [Kenny Dorham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenny_Dorham "Kenny Dorham"), and [Willie Bobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Bobo "Willie Bobo") released latin jazz albums. [Willie Bobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Bobo "Willie Bobo") fused [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), latin, and R&B music.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_jazz#cite_note-11) ### Jazz in-clave \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Latin_jazz&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Jazz in-clave")\] [... middle omitted — see footer ...] | show

[Jump to content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#bodyContent) From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (Redirected from [Jazz-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz-rock&redirect=no "Jazz-rock")) Music genre combining jazz methods with rock music, funk, and rhythm and blues | Jazz fusion | | --- | | Other names | - Jazz rock
- jazz-rock fusion
- fusion | | Stylistic origins | - [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz")
