- [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") | | Cultural origins | Late 1960s, United States | | Derivative forms | - [Zeuhl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeuhl "Zeuhl")[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-1)
- [smooth jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz "Smooth jazz")
- [acid jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid_jazz "Acid jazz")
- [quiet storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiet_storm "Quiet storm")
- [urban contemporary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_contemporary "Urban contemporary")
- [nu jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nu_jazz "Nu jazz") | | Other topics | | - [List of musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_jazz_fusion_musicians "List of jazz fusion musicians") | **Jazz fusion** (also known as **jazz rock**, **jazz-rock fusion**, or simply **fusion**[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-2)) is a [popular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music") [genre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_genre "Music genre") that developed in the late 1960s when musicians combined [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") harmony and [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_improvisation "Jazz improvisation") with [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), and [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues"). [Electric guitars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar") and [basses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar"), [amplifiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_amplifier "Guitar amplifier"), and [keyboard instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyboard_instrument "Keyboard instrument") (including [electric pianos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_piano "Electric piano") and [organs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_organ "Electric organ")) that were popular in rock began to be used by jazz musicians, particularly those who had grown up listening to rock and roll. Jazz fusion [arrangements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangements "Arrangements") vary in complexity. Some employ groove-based vamps fixed to a single key or a single chord with a simple, repeated melody. Others use elaborate [chord progressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_progression "Chord progression"), unconventional time signatures, or melodies with [counter-melodies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hauptstimme "Hauptstimme"), in a similar fashion to [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock"). These arrangements, whether simple or complex, typically include improvised sections that can vary in length, much like in other forms of jazz. As with jazz, jazz fusion can employ brass and [woodwind instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodwind_instrument "Woodwind instrument") such as trumpet and saxophone, but other instruments often substitute for these. A jazz fusion band is less likely to use acoustic [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano "Piano") and [double bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_bass "Double bass"), and more likely to use electric guitars, electric pianos, organs, [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer"), and [bass guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar"). The term "jazz rock" is sometimes used as a synonym for "jazz fusion" and for music performed by late 1960s- and 1970s-era rock bands that added jazz elements to their music. After a decade of popularity during the 1970s, fusion expanded its improvisatory and experimental approaches through the 1980s in parallel with the development of a radio-friendly style called [smooth jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_jazz "Smooth jazz").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-3) Experimentation continued in the 1990s and 2000s. Fusion albums, even those that are made by the same group or artist, may include a variety of musical styles. Rather than being a codified musical style, fusion can be viewed as a musical tradition or approach. ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: History")\] | | | | --- | --- | | ![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Ambox_current_red_Asia_Australia.svg/60px-Ambox_current_red_Asia_Australia.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail) | This section needs to be **updated**. The reason given is: **Does not cover other decades besides the 70s and out of touch with recent developments**. Please help update this article to reflect recent events or newly available information._(November 2023)_ | ### Origins \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_fusion&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Origins")\] When [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") died in 1967, rock was the most popular music in America, and _[DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat")_ magazine went so far as to declare in a headline that: "Jazz as We Know It Is Dead".[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Fusions-4) [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") states that "until around 1967, the worlds of jazz and rock were nearly completely separate",[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-Fusion_overview-5) although the [Daevid Allen Trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_Machine "Soft Machine") which later became the Soft Machine formed in 1963,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion#cite_note-6) while the jazz label [Verve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verve_Records "Verve Records") released the influential debut album, _[Freak Out!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freak_Out! # Modal jazz Modal jazz Sub-genre of jazz | | | | --- | --- | | [![icon](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/6/6c/Wiki_letter_w.svg/120px-Wiki_letter_w.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wiki_letter_w.svg) | This article **is missing information** about modulation. Please expand the article to include this information. Further details may exist on the [talk page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:Modal_jazz "Talk:Modal jazz")._(January 2022)_ | | Modal jazz | | --- | | Cultural origins | Mid-1950s, United States | | Typical instruments | - [Clarinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarinet "Clarinet")
- [saxophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxophone "Saxophone")
- [trumpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trumpet "Trumpet")
- [trombone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trombone "Trombone")
- [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano "Piano")
- [double bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_bass "Double bass")
- [drums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum "Drum")
- [keyboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_keyboard "Musical keyboard")
- [electric guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar")
- [acoustic guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_guitar "Acoustic guitar") | **Modal jazz** is [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") that makes use of [musical modes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mode_(music) "Mode (music)"), often [modulating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulation_(music) "Modulation (music)") among them to accompany the [chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_(music) "Chord (music)") instead of relying on one [tonal center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonic_(music) "Tonic (music)") used across the piece. Though exerting influence to the present, modal jazz was most popular in the 1950s and 1960s, as evidenced by the success of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")'s 1958 composition " [Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(composition) "Milestones (composition)")" and 1959 album _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_, and [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane")'s quartet from 1960 to 1965. Other performers of modal jazz include [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea"), [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans"), [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson"), [Bobby Hutcherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Hutcherson "Bobby Hutcherson"), [Pharoah Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharoah_Sanders "Pharoah Sanders"), [Woody Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woody_Shaw "Woody Shaw"), [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter"), [McCoy Tyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCoy_Tyner "McCoy Tyner"), and [Larry Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Young_(musician) "Larry Young (musician)").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-Essential-1) ## History In [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") as well as in [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"), musicians use chords to provide the background for solos. A piece starts out with a theme that introduces a series of chords for the solos. These chords repeat throughout the whole piece, while the soloists play new, improvised themes over the repeated [chord progression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_progression "Chord progression"). By the 1950s, improvising over chords had become such a dominant part of jazz that sidemen at recording dates were sometimes given nothing more than a list of chords to play from.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-2) [Mercer Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer_Ellington "Mercer Ellington") has stated that [Juan Tizol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Tizol "Juan Tizol") conceived the melody to " [Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(1937_song) "Caravan (1937 song)")" in 1936 as a result of his days studying music in Puerto Rico, where they could not afford much sheet music so the teacher would turn the music upside down after they had learned to play it right-side up.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-mercer1994-3) This "inversion" technique led to a modal sound throughout Tizol's work.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-mercer1994-3) [Sun Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Ra "Sun Ra") reportedly rehearsed a small group consisting of [Harold Ousley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Ousley "Harold Ousley"), [Vernel Fournier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernel_Fournier "Vernel Fournier"), and [Wilbur Ware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Ware "Wilbur Ware") in 1950 that played original songs that were modal in which the melody was based on a single chord or [vamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostinato#Vamp "Ostinato") – ten years before this approach became popular in jazz.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-4) Saxophonist [Wayne Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Shorter "Wayne Shorter") has noted that the 1953 composition " [Glass Enclosure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_Enclosure "Glass Enclosure")" by pianist Bud Powell was one of the earliest jazz compositions to make use of [Lydian chords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_chord "Lydian chord"), based on the [Lydian mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydian_mode "Lydian mode") that was not widely used in jazz until about a decade later.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-5) Powell's 1951 [Un Poco Loco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Un_Poco_Loco "Un Poco Loco") uses the Lydian chords and even uses Lydian chords stacked on top of each implying a [polytonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytonality "Polytonality") (D [major 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_seventh_chord "Major seventh chord") over C major 7: CEGBDF#AC#) with the improvisation based on alternating Lydian-ish polytonality and an [altered dominant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altered_dominant "Altered dominant") chord.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-6) Towards the end of the 1950s, spurred by the experiments of composer and bandleader George Russell, musicians began using a modal approach. They chose not to write their pieces using conventional chord changes, but instead using modes. Musicians employing this technique include Miles Davis, [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), Bill Evans, [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), and Wayne Shorter. [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.png/500px-Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.png) Opening chord to " [Maiden Voyage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiden_Voyage_(composition) "Maiden Voyage (composition)")": minor [eleventh chord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleventh_chord "Eleventh chord") (Am9/D).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-What-7)[Play](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/9e/Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.mid/Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.mid.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Minor_eleventh_chord_Herbie_Hancock_Maiden_Voyage.mid "File:Minor eleventh chord Herbie Hancock Maiden Voyage.mid") Using D [Dorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorian_mode#Modern_Dorian_mode "Dorian mode").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz#cite_note-8) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] | Related | - [Acid jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid_jazz "Acid jazz")

- [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music") | **Free improvisation** (also known as **free-form music**) is a form of [improvised music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") centered on a commitment to non- [idiomatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idiomatic_(music) "Idiomatic (music)") musical expression.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-1) It developed through [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [serialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serialism "Serialism") and [indeterminacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indeterminacy_(music) "Indeterminacy (music)"), and is characterized by a general rejection of formal [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory") and [tonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonality "Tonality"), instead following the intuition of its performers and the exploration of dynamic, timbre and texture. The term can refer to both a technique—employed by any musician in any genre—and as a recognizable genre of [experimental music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_music "Experimental music") in its own right. Free improvisation, as a genre of music, developed primarily in the U.K. as well as the U.S. and Europe in the mid to late 1960s, largely as an outgrowth of [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") and [contemporary classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_classical_music "Contemporary classical music"). Exponents of free improvised music include the improvising groups [AMM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMM_(group) "AMM (group)") and [Spontaneous Music Ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_Music_Ensemble "Spontaneous Music Ensemble"), as well as solo instrumentalists such as saxophonists [Evan Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Parker "Evan Parker"), [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton"), [Peter Brötzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Br%C3%B6tzmann "Peter Brötzmann") and [John Zorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Zorn "John Zorn"), trombonist [George E. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_E._Lewis "George E. Lewis"), guitarists [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)"), [Henry Kaiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kaiser_(musician) "Henry Kaiser (musician)"), [Fred Frith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Frith "Fred Frith"), [Taku Sugimoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taku_Sugimoto "Taku Sugimoto") and [Toshimaru Nakamura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toshimaru_Nakamura "Toshimaru Nakamura"), bassists [Damon Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damon_Smith "Damon Smith") and [Jair-Rohm Parker Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jair-Rohm_Parker_Wells "Jair-Rohm Parker Wells"), and composer [Pauline Oliveros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Oliveros "Pauline Oliveros"). ## Characteristics \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_improvisation&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Characteristics")\] In the context of [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory"), free improvisation denotes the shift from a focus on [harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony") and structure to other dimensions of music, such as [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre"), [texture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texture_(music) "Texture (music)"), melodic intervals, [rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm "Rhythm") and spontaneous musical interactions between performers. This can give free improvised music abstract and nondescript qualities.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-2) Although individual performers may choose to play in a certain style or [key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_signature "Key signature"), or at certain [tempos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo"), conventions such as song structures are highly uncommon; more emphasis is generally placed on the [mood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mood_(psychology) "Mood (psychology)") of the music, or on performative gestures, than on preset forms of [melody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody "Melody"), harmony or [rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm "Rhythm"). These elements are improvised at will as the music progresses, and performers will often intuitively react to each other based on the elements of their performance. English guitarist [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)") described free improvisation as "playing without memory".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-3) In his book _Improvisation_, Bailey wrote that free improvisation "has no stylistic or idiomatic commitment. It has no prescribed idiomatic sound. The characteristics of freely improvised music are established only by the sonic musical identity of the person or persons playing it."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation#cite_note-4) Free music performers from disparate backgrounds often engage musically with other [genres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_genres_of_music "List of genres of music"). For example, Italian composer [Ennio Morricone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ennio_Morricone "Ennio Morricone") was a member of the free improvisation group Nuova Consonanza. [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton") has written [opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera "Opera"), and [John Zorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Zorn "John Zorn") has written acclaimed orchestral pieces. ## History \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Free_improvisation&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: History")\] Though there are many important precedents and developments, free improvisation developed gradually, making it difficult to pinpoint a single moment when the style was born. Free improvisation primarily descends from the [Indeterminacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indeterminacy_(music) "Indeterminacy (music)") movement and [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"). - [math rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Math_rock "Math rock") | | Local scenes | | [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") | **Loft jazz** (also known as the **loft scene** or **loft era**) was a cultural music phenomenon that occurred in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") during the mid-1970s. ## Description [Gary Giddins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Giddins "Gary Giddins") described it as follows: "\[A\] new coterie of avant-garde musicians took much of the jazz world by surprise... \[T\]hey interpreted the idea of freedom as the capacity to choose between all the realms of jazz, mixing and matching them not only with each other, but with old and new pop, R&B and rock, classical music and world music... \[S\]eemingly overnight new venues - in many instances, apartments or lofts (hence the phrase 'loft jazz') - opened shop to present their wares."[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-1) According to Michael Heller, "lofts were not an organization, nor a movement, nor an ideology, nor a genre, nor a neighborhood, nor a lineage of individuals. They were, instead, a meeting point, a locus for interaction."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-2) Heller stated that "loft practices came to be defined by a number of key characteristics, including (1) low admission charges or suggested donations, (2) casual atmospheres that blurred the distinction between performer and audience, (3) ownership / administration by musicians, and (4) mixed-use spaces that combined both private living areas and public presentation space."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-3) Regarding the music played in these venues, Michael J. Agovino wrote: "This was community music. Part of the point was that, free of the strictures of clubs, the music could be anything, go anywhere, go on for as long as it wanted."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-4) David Such stated that "the cutting contests, personality cults, and vices that characterized the jazz scene of the 1940s and 1950s were mostly missing."[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-5) The scene was reviewed and documented by Giddins, Peter Occhiogrosso[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-6) of the [SoHo Weekly News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoHo_Weekly_News "SoHo Weekly News"), [Leroi Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amiri_Baraka "Amiri Baraka"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-7) [Robert Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Palmer_(author/producer) "Robert Palmer (author/producer)"),[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-8) and [Stanley Crouch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Crouch "Stanley Crouch").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-9) Coinciding with this activity was an influx of musicians from outside New York. Newcomers from Chicago included a group associated with the [AACM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians "Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians"); these included [Muhal Richard Abrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhal_Richard_Abrams "Muhal Richard Abrams"), [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton"), [Kalaparusha Maurice McIntyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalaparusha_Maurice_McIntyre "Kalaparusha Maurice McIntyre"), [Lester Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bowie "Lester Bowie"), [Amina Claudine Myers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amina_Claudine_Myers "Amina Claudine Myers"), [Henry Threadgill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Threadgill "Henry Threadgill"), [Steve McCall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_McCall_(drummer) "Steve McCall (drummer)"), [Fred Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Hopkins "Fred Hopkins"), [Chico Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chico_Freeman "Chico Freeman"), [Malachi Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malachi_Thompson "Malachi Thompson"), and [George E. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_E._Lewis "George E. Lewis"). Various members of the [Black Artists Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group "Black Artists Group") came from St. Louis, including [Charles "Bobo" Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_%22Bobo%22_Shaw "Charles \"Bobo\" Shaw"), [Baikida Carroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikida_Carroll "Baikida Carroll"), [Oliver Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Lake "Oliver Lake"), [Julius Hemphill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Hemphill "Julius Hemphill"), [Hamiet Bluiett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiet_Bluiett "Hamiet Bluiett"), [J. D. Parran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._D._Parran "J. D. Parran"), and [Joseph Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bowie "Joseph Bowie"). Members of [Horace Tapscott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott "Horace Tapscott")'s [UGMAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_God's_Musicians_and_Artists_Ascension "Union of God's Musicians and Artists Ascension"), such as [Arthur Blythe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Blythe "Arthur Blythe"), [David Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Murray_(saxophonist) "David Murray (saxophonist)"), and [Butch Morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butch_Morris "Butch Morris"), arrived from California. All of these, plus many local musicians, participated in the loft scene to some degree.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_jazz#cite_note-10) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] 09. - [Phil Cohran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Cohran "Phil Cohran") | | Type | Non-profit organization | | Location | - Chicago, Illinois | | Region served | U.S. | | Official language | English | | Key people | - [Henry Threadgill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Threadgill "Henry Threadgill")
- [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton")
- [Roscoe Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscoe_Mitchell "Roscoe Mitchell") | | Affiliations | [Black Artists Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group "Black Artists Group") | | [Endowment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_endowment "Financial endowment") | [MacArthur Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Foundation "MacArthur Foundation") | | Website | [aacmchicago.org](http://aacmchicago.org/) | Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians The **Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians** ( **AACM**) is an American [nonprofit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_organization "Nonprofit organization"), founded in 1965 in Chicago by pianist [Muhal Richard Abrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhal_Richard_Abrams "Muhal Richard Abrams"), pianist [Jodie Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jodie_Christian "Jodie Christian"), drummer [Steve McCall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_McCall_(drummer) "Steve McCall (drummer)"), and composer [Phil Cohran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Cohran "Phil Cohran").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-RCJE-1) The AACM is devoted "to nurturing, performing, and recording serious, original music," according to its charter. It supports and encourages [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") performers, composers and educators. Although founded in the jazz tradition, the group's outreach and influence has, according to Larry Blumenfeld, "touched nearly all corners of modern music."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-2) Per the AACM, it "pays homage to the diverse styles of expression within the body of Black Music in the USA, Africa and throughout the world."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-AACMaboutPage-2022-3) ## Background \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Background")\] By the 1960s, jazz music was losing ground to rock music, and the founders of the AACM felt that a proactive group of musicians would add creativity and outlet for new music.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-Reich-4) The AACM was formed in May 1965 by a group of African-American musicians in Chicago centered on [pianist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pianist "Pianist") [Muhal Richard Abrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhal_Richard_Abrams "Muhal Richard Abrams"), who had organized the Experimental Band since 1961.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-LarkinGE-5) The musicians were generally steadfast in their commitment to their music, despite a lack of performance venues and sometimes indifferent audiences. From 1969 the AACM organised a music education program for inner-city youths.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-6) In the 1960s and 1970s AACM members were among the most important and innovative in all of jazz, though the AACM's contemporary influence has waned some in recent years. Many AACM members have recorded widely: in the early days on the [Delmark Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delmark_Records "Delmark Records") Avant Garde Jazz series and later on the [Black Saint/Soul Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Saint/Soul_Note "Black Saint/Soul Note") and [India Navigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_Navigation "India Navigation") labels, and to a lesser extent on the [Arista Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arista_Records "Arista Records") and [ECM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECM_(record_label) "ECM (record label)") labels.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-7) The musical endeavors of members of the AACM often include an adventurous mixing of avant-garde jazz, classical, and world music. The AACM also ran a school, The AACM School of Music, with classes in all areas taught by members of the AACM. The AACM also had a strong relationship with an influential sister organization, the [Black Artists Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group "Black Artists Group") (BAG) of [St. Louis, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis,_Missouri "St. Louis, Missouri").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-LarkinJazz-8) The AACM has received aid from the [MacArthur Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Foundation "MacArthur Foundation") and has a strong relationship with [Columbia College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_College_Chicago "Columbia College Chicago"). _A Power Stronger Than Itself: The AACM and American Experimental Music_ by AACM member [George E. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_E._Lewis "George E. Lewis"), which documents the AACM's history, has been published by the University of Chicago Press (May 2008).[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-nyt_2008-9) In 2015, a 50-year retrospective exhibition of art, music and group-related artifacts, entitled, "Free at First", was held at the [DuSable Museum of African American History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuSable_Museum_of_African_American_History "DuSable Museum of African American History").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-Reich-4) ## Music \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Music")\] The AACM has been on the forefront of the [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") since its inception in 1965. [Anthony Braxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Braxton "Anthony Braxton"), [Henry Threadgill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Threadgill "Henry Threadgill"), and the [Art Ensemble of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Ensemble_of_Chicago "Art Ensemble of Chicago") pushed the boundaries of jazz and challenged the avant-garde classical movement led by [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage"). Concerts were heavily improvised, and many AACM members created scores that blended music, geometry, painting, and ciphers to be interpreted by the performers live. The AACM was part of an artistic movement on the South Side of Chicago that included AFRICobra (African Commune of Bad Relevant Artists) and other collectives.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-10) In the third decade of the 21st century, AACM members continue to produce vibrant avant-garde jazz and jazz-influenced music in Chicago and elsewhere.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] ## Members \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Members")\] (some deceased; largely complete through at least early 2026) [\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-AACM-TShirt-2025-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-12) - [Muhal Richard Abrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhal_Richard_Abrams "Muhal Richard Abrams")[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Creative_Musicians#cite_note-LarkinGE-5) - Top Questions


- What is jazz-rock music?







Jazz-rock is a popular music style blending modern jazz improvisation with rock music's bass lines, drumming, and instrumentation. It emphasizes electronic instruments and dance rhythms.



Since the 1920s, fusions of jazz and popular music existed, contrasting jazz's qualities with popular music. In the 1960s, jazz tunes started incorporating rock rhythms. By 1969, artists like Miles Davis, Tony Williams, and John McLaughlin created distinctive fusion music contrasting jazz and rock elements.



In the early 1970s, bands such as Mahavishnu Orchestra, Headhunters, and Weather Report further explored this style. This music gained a large audience and was known as crossover, appealing to both jazz and popular music fans.

- Which styles of music are combined in jazz-rock?







Jazz-rock combines modern [jazz](https://www.britannica.com/art/jazz/Introduction#ref1) improvisation with [rock music](https://www.britannica.com/art/rock-music/Crucial-rock-musicians#ref93483)'s bass lines, drumming styles, and instrumentation, with a strong emphasis on electronic instruments and dance rhythms. It contrasted and enhanced jazz and rock elements. Jazz-rock is also known as crossover because sales of the music crossed over from the jazz market to the popular music market.



Other fusions combined hard bop, the funky 1960s jazz, and rock tunes over which they improvised jazz.

- When did jazz-rock become popular?







Jazz-rock, a fusion of modern jazz improvisation with rock music elements, gained popularity by the early 1970s. This musical form incorporates the bass lines, drumming styles, and instrumentation of rock, with a strong emphasis on electronic instruments and dance rhythms.



Figures like Miles Davis, along with associates such as John McLaughlin, Wayne Shorter, and Herbie Hancock, pioneered this distinctive fusion. Davis's 1969 album, _In a Silent Way_, is often regarded as the seminal album of the jazz fusion movement, and his subsequent work, _Bitches Brew_, further embraced rock elements, influencing groups like Weather Report and Chick Corea’s Return to Forever.



Although some critics dismissed Davis's post- _Bitches Brew_ music, his efforts helped maintain jazz's popularity with mainstream audiences. The style became known as crossover because sales of the music crossed over from the jazz market to the popular music market.

- How do musicians blend jazz and rock elements in jazz-rock music?







Jazz-rock blends jazz improvisation with rock's bass lines, drumming, and instrumentation, heavily featuring electronic instruments and dance rhythms. In the 1960s, jazz musicians started incorporating rock rhythms into their music.



Figures like Miles Davis, Tony Williams, and John McLaughlin contrasted and enhanced jazz and rock elements. Other artists mixed hard bop with rock tunes, while some experimented with free jazz fusion, though the latter sometimes overshadowed jazz improvisation due to rock's repetitive patterns.

(m.1954;div.1964)​ | Musical artist **Randolph Denard Ornette Coleman** (March 9, 1930 – June 11, 2015)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Ratliff-1) was an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") saxophonist, trumpeter, violinist, and composer. He is best known as a principal founder of the [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") genre, a term derived from his 1960 album _[Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation")_. His pioneering works often abandoned the [harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony")-based composition, [tonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonality "Tonality"), chord changes, and fixed rhythm found in earlier jazz idioms;[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-2) instead, Coleman emphasized an experimental approach to [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisation "Improvisation") rooted in ensemble playing and [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") phrasing.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) Thom Jurek of [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called him "one of the most beloved and polarizing figures in jazz history", noting that while "now celebrated as a fearless innovator and a genius, he was initially regarded by peers and critics as rebellious, disruptive, and even a fraud."[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) Born and raised in [Fort Worth, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas "Fort Worth, Texas"), Coleman taught himself to play the saxophone when he was a teenager.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Ratliff-1) He began his musical career playing in local [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") groups and eventually formed his own jazz group in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), featuring members such as [Ed Blackwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Blackwell "Ed Blackwell"), [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), and [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins"). In November 1959, his quartet began a controversial residency at the [Five Spot Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Spot_Caf%C3%A9 "Five Spot Café") in New York City and he released the influential album _[The Shape of Jazz to Come](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come "The Shape of Jazz to Come")_ on [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records"). Coleman's subsequent Atlantic releases in the early 1960s would profoundly impact the direction of jazz in that decade, and his compositions " [Lonely Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonely_Woman_(composition) "Lonely Woman (composition)")" and " [Broadway Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_Blues_(Coleman) "Broadway Blues (Coleman)")" became [standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard") cited as important early works in free jazz.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-HellmerLawn2005-4) In the mid 1960s, Coleman left Atlantic for other labels, including [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") and [Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), and began performing with his young son [Denardo Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denardo_Coleman "Denardo Coleman") on drums. He explored symphonic composition with his 1972 album _[Skies of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skies_of_America "Skies of America")_, featuring the [London Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Symphony_Orchestra "London Symphony Orchestra"). In the mid-1970s, he formed the group [Prime Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Time_(band) "Prime Time (band)"), which performed electric [jazz-funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz-funk "Jazz-funk") and elaborated on his theory of [harmolodics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmolodics "Harmolodics").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-allmusicbio-3) In 1995, he and Denardo founded the [Harmolodic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmolodics#Record_label "Harmolodics") record label. Coleman's 2006 album _[Sound Grammar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_Grammar "Sound Grammar")_ received the 2007 [Pulitzer Prize for Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Music "Pulitzer Prize for Music"), making him the second jazz musician ever to receive the honor.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-5) ## Biography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Biography")\] ### Early life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ornette_Coleman&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Early life")\] Coleman was born Randolph Denard Ornette Coleman on March 9, 1930, in [Fort Worth, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas "Fort Worth, Texas"),[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Fordham-6) where he was raised.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Atlantic1972-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-EGP-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Litweiler-9) He attended [I.M. Terrell High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I.M._Terrell_High_School "I.M. Terrell High School") in Fort Worth, where he participated in the band program until he was dismissed for improvising during [John Philip Sousa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Philip_Sousa "John Philip Sousa")'s march " [The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post_(march) "The Washington Post (march)")". He began performing [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") on tenor saxophone, and formed The Jam Jivers with [Prince Lasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Lasha "Prince Lasha") and [Charles Moffett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Moffett "Charles Moffett").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman#cite_note-Litweiler-9) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] - [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), New York, U.S. | | Genres | [Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz"), [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [free improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation") | | Occupations | Musician, bandleader, composer, improviser, poet | | Instrument | Piano | | Years active | 1956–2018 | | Labels | [Transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transition_Records "Transition Records"), [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records"), [Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_Records "Freedom Records"), [Hathut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hathut_Records "Hathut Records"), [Enja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enja_Records "Enja Records"), [FMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FMP/Free_Music_Production "FMP/Free Music Production") | Musical artist **Cecil Percival Taylor** (March 25, 1929–April 5, 2018)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Such-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Feather-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Seisdedos-3) was an American pianist and poet.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-FOOTNOTESuch199361-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Yanow-5) Taylor was [classically trained](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classically_trained "Classically trained") and was one of the pioneers of [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"). His music is characterized by an energetic, physical approach, resulting in complex [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_improvisation "Musical improvisation") often involving [tone clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tone_clusters "Tone clusters") and intricate [polyrhythms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyrhythms "Polyrhythms"). His technique has been compared to [percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_instrument "Percussion instrument"). Referring to the number of keys on a standard piano, [Val Wilmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Wilmer "Val Wilmer") used the phrase "eighty-eight tuned drums" to describe Taylor's style.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-6) He has been referred to as " [Art Tatum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Tatum "Art Tatum") with contemporary-classical leanings".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-Tatum-7) ## Early life and education \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")\] Cecil Percival Taylor was born on March 25, 1929, in [Long Island City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_City "Long Island City"), [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens "Queens"),[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-nytobit-8) and raised in [Corona, Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona,_Queens "Corona, Queens").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-NYT2012-9) As an only child in a middle-class family, Taylor was encouraged by his mother, Almeda Ragland Taylor, to play music at an early age. He began playing piano at age six and went on to study at the [New York College of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_College_of_Music "New York College of Music") and [New England Conservatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Conservatory "New England Conservatory") in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"). At the New England Conservatory, Taylor majored in popular music arrangement. During his time there, he also became familiar with contemporary European [art music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_music "Art music"). [Bela Bartók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_Bart%C3%B3k "Béla Bartók") and [Karlheinz Stockhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlheinz_Stockhausen "Karlheinz Stockhausen") notably influenced his music.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-:0-10) In 1955, Taylor moved back to New York City from Boston. He formed a quartet with soprano saxophonist [Steve Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lacy_(saxophonist) "Steve Lacy (saxophonist)"), bassist [Buell Neidlinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buell_Neidlinger "Buell Neidlinger"), and drummer [Dennis Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Charles "Denis Charles").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-:0-10) Taylor's first recording, _[Jazz Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Advance "Jazz Advance")_, featured Lacy and was released in 1956.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-11) The recording is described by [Richard Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Cook_(journalist) "Richard Cook (journalist)") and [Brian Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Morton_(Scottish_writer) "Brian Morton (Scottish writer)") in the _[Penguin Guide to Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Guide_to_Jazz "Penguin Guide to Jazz")_: "While there are still many nods to conventional [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop") form in this set, it already points to the freedoms in which the pianist would later immerse himself."[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-12) Taylor's quartet featuring Lacy also appeared at the 1957 [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival"), which was made into the album _[At Newport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/At_Newport_(Cecil_Taylor_and_Gigi_Gryce_album) "At Newport (Cecil Taylor and Gigi Gryce album)")_.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-13) Taylor collaborated with saxophonist [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") in 1958 on _[Stereo Drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereo_Drive "Stereo Drive")_, now available as _Coltrane Time_.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-14) ## 1950s and early 1960s \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cecil_Taylor&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: 1950s and early 1960s")\] Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, Taylor's music grew more complex and moved away from existing jazz styles. Gigs were often hard to come by, and club owners found that Taylor's approach of playing long pieces tended to impede business.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-15) His 1959 [LP record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record") _[Looking Ahead!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looking_Ahead! "Looking Ahead!")_ showcased his innovation as a creator as compared to the jazz mainstream. Unlike others at the time, Taylor utilized virtuosic techniques and made swift stylistic shifts from phrase to phrase. These qualities, among others, still remained notable distinctions of his music for the rest of his life.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor#cite_note-16) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] - He is among the most influential and acclaimed figures in the [history of jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz#Post-war_jazz "Jazz") and 20th-century music. Born and raised in [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), Coltrane moved to [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") after high school, where he immersed himself in the local jazz scene, studied music, and served in the [Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy") toward the end of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") before making his professional debut in 1945. Working in the [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") and [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop") idioms early in his career, Coltrane helped pioneer the use of [modes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz") and was one of the players at the forefront of [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"). He led at least fifty recording sessions and appeared on many albums by other musicians, including trumpeter [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis") and pianist [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk"). Over the course of his career, Coltrane's music took on an increasingly spiritual dimension, as exemplified on his most acclaimed album _[A Love Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Love_Supreme "A Love Supreme")_ (1965) and others.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-1) Decades after his death, Coltrane remains influential, and he has received numerous posthumous awards, including a [special Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_Special_Citations_and_Awards "Pulitzer Prize Special Citations and Awards"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-pulitzer-2) and he was [canonized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonization "Canonization") by the [African Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Orthodox_Church "African Orthodox Church"). His second wife was pianist and harpist [Alice Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Coltrane "Alice Coltrane"). The couple had three children: John Jr. (1964-1982), a bassist;[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-3) [Ravi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravi_Coltrane "Ravi Coltrane") (born 1965), a saxophonist; and Oran (born 1967), a saxophonist, guitarist, drummer, and singer.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane#cite_note-6) ## Biography ### 1926–1945: Early life [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/U.S._Naval_Reserve_portrait_of_Johnny_Coltrane_edit.jpg/500px-U.S._Naval_Reserve_portrait_of_Johnny_Coltrane_edit.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:U.S._Naval_Reserve_portrait_of_Johnny_Coltrane_edit.jpg) Coltrane's first recordings were made when he was a sailor. # Albert Ayler Albert Ayler American jazz saxophonist (1936–1970) | Albert Ayler | | --- | | [![Photograph of a man with a short afro hairstyle and short goatee playing saxophone, arching his back to raise the instrument above his head](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Albert_Ayler_%281967%E2%80%9368_photo_portrait_for_ABC_Impulse%21%29.jpg/500px-Albert_Ayler_%281967%E2%80%9368_photo_portrait_for_ABC_Impulse%21%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Albert_Ayler_(1967%E2%80%9368_photo_portrait_for_ABC_Impulse!).jpg "Photograph of a man with a short afro hairstyle and short goatee playing saxophone, arching his back to raise the instrument above his head")

Records"), Ayler | Musical artist **Albert Ayler** ([/ˈaɪlər/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); July 13, 1936– November 25, 1970) was an American [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") saxophonist and composer.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-RCJE-1) After early experience playing [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") and [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"), Ayler began recording music during the [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") era of the 1960s. However, some critics argue that while Ayler's style is undeniably original and unorthodox, it does not adhere to the generally accepted critical understanding of free jazz.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Mandel-2) In fact, Ayler's style is difficult to categorize, and it evoked incredibly strong and disparate reactions from critics and fans alike.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Claghorn-3) His innovations have inspired many subsequent jazz musicians.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Mandel-2) His trio and quartet records of 1964, such as _[Spiritual Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity "Spiritual Unity")_ and _[The Hilversum Session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hilversum_Session "The Hilversum Session")_, show him advancing the improvisational notions of [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") and [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") into abstract realms where whole [timbre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre "Timbre"), and not just mainly [harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony") with [melody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody "Melody"), is the music's backbone. His ecstatic music of 1965 and 1966, such as "Spirits Rejoice" and "Truth Is Marching In", has been compared by critics to the sound of a [brass band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brass_band#New_Orleans "Brass band"), and involved simple, march-like themes which alternated with wild group [improvisations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_improvisation "Free improvisation") and were regarded as retrieving jazz's pre- [Louis Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Armstrong "Louis Armstrong") roots.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-4) ## Biography ### Early life and career Born in [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland "Cleveland"), Ohio, and raised in [Shaker Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaker_Heights "Shaker Heights"),[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-5) Ayler was first taught alto saxophone by his father Edward, who was a semiprofessional saxophonist and violinist. Edward and Albert played alto saxophone duets in church and often listened to jazz records together, including swing era jazz and then-new bop albums.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Claghorn-3) Ayler's upbringing in the church had a great impact on his life and music, and much of his music can be understood as an attempt to express his spirituality, including the aptly titled _[Spiritual Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity "Spiritual Unity")_, and his album of spirituals, _Goin' Home_, which features "meandering" solos that are meant to be treated as meditations on sacred texts, and at some points as "speaking in tongues" with his saxophone.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Whitehead-6) Ayler's experience in the church and exposure to swing jazz artists also impacted his sound: his wide vibrato was similar to that of gospel saxophonists, who sought a more vocal-like sound with their instruments, and to that of brass players in New Orleans swing bands.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Whitehead-6) Ayler attended [John Adams High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams_High_School_(Cleveland,_Ohio) "John Adams High School (Cleveland, Ohio)") on Cleveland's East Side, and graduated in 1954 at the age of 18. He later studied at [Academy Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Music_(Cleveland,_Ohio)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Academy Music (Cleveland, Ohio)") in Cleveland with jazz saxophonist [Benny Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Miller?action=edit&redlink=1 "Benny Miller"). Ayler also played the [oboe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oboe "Oboe") in high school. As a teenager, Ayler's understanding of bebop style and mastery of standard repertoire earned him the nickname of "Little Bird", after [Charlie "Bird" Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), in the small Cleveland jazz scene.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-7) In 1952, at the age of 16, Ayler began playing bar-walking, honking, [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B")-style tenor with blues singer and harmonica player [Little Walter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Walter "Little Walter"), spending two summer vacations with Walter's band.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Litweiler152-8) In 1958, after graduating from high school, Ayler joined the United States Army, where he switched from alto to tenor sax and jammed with other enlisted musicians, including tenor saxophonist [Stanley Turrentine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Turrentine "Stanley Turrentine"). Ayler also played in the regiment band, along with future composer [Harold Budd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Budd "Harold Budd").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-9) In 1959 he was stationed in France, where he was further exposed to the martial music that would be a core influence on his later work. After his discharge from the army, Ayler tried to find work in Los Angeles and Cleveland, but his increasingly iconoclastic playing, which had moved away from traditional harmony, was not welcomed by traditionalists.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler#cite_note-Litweiler152-8) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] Biography, Holy Ghost by Richard Koloda. - [Miles Davis Quintet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis_Quintet "Miles Davis Quintet") | | | | Website | [milesdavis.com](https://milesdavis.com/) | | Signature | | [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Miles_Davis_Signature.svg/250px-Miles_Davis_Signature.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis_Signature.svg) | **Miles Dewey Davis III** (May 26, 1926–September 28, 1991) was an American trumpeter, bandleader, composer, and painter.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-1) He is among the most influential and acclaimed figures in the history of [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") and [20th-century music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th-century_music "20th-century music"). In a career spanning nearly five decades, Davis was at the forefront of several major stylistic developments in jazz, including [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"), [cool jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cool_jazz "Cool jazz"), [hard bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_bop "Hard bop"), [third stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_stream "Third stream"), [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"), [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") and [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-allmusic-2) His legacy extends into [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), [classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music") and [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"). Born into an affluent family in [Alton, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alton,_Illinois "Alton, Illinois"), and raised in [East St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_St._Louis "East St. Louis"), Davis started on the trumpet in his early teens. He left to study at the [Juilliard School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juilliard_School "Juilliard School") in New York City, before dropping out and making his professional debut as a member of saxophonist [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker")'s bebop quintet from 1944 to 1948. Shortly afterwards, he recorded the _[Birth of the Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_of_the_Cool "Birth of the Cool")_ sessions for [Capitol Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Records "Capitol Records"), which were instrumental to the development of cool jazz. In the early 1950s, Davis recorded some of the earliest hard bop music under [Prestige Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestige_Records "Prestige Records"). After a widely acclaimed comeback performance at the [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival"), he signed a long-term contract with [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"), and recorded the album _['Round About Midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'Round_About_Midnight "'Round About Midnight")_ in 1955.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYanow2005176-3) It was his first work with saxophonist [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") and bassist [Paul Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Chambers "Paul Chambers"), key members of the sextet he led into the early 1960s. During this period, he alternated between orchestral jazz collaborations with arranger [Gil Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Evans "Gil Evans"), such as the [Spanish music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Spain "Music of Spain")–influenced _[Sketches of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sketches_of_Spain "Sketches of Spain")_ (1960), and band recordings, such as _[Milestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milestones_(Miles_Davis_album) "Milestones (Miles Davis album)")_ (1958) and _[Kind of Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kind_of_Blue "Kind of Blue")_ (1959).[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-aar-4) The latter recording remains one of the most popular jazz albums of all time,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCurdy200461-5) having sold more than five million copies in the U.S. alone and 6.4 million copies worldwide. - [United Artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Artists_Records "United Artists Records") | | | | Website | [www.charlesmingus.com](https://www.charlesmingus.com/) | Musical artist **Charles Mingus Jr.** (April 22, 1922 – January 5, 1979) was an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") [upright bassist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_bass "Double bass"), [composer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composer "Composer"), [bandleader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandleader "Bandleader"), [pianist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pianist "Pianist"), and author. A major proponent of collective [improvisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_improvisation "Jazz improvisation"), he is considered one of the greatest jazz musicians and composers in history,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-Underdog-1) with a career spanning three decades and collaborations with other jazz greats, such as [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington"), [Charlie Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Parker "Charlie Parker"), [Max Roach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Roach "Max Roach"), and [Eric Dolphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Dolphy "Eric Dolphy"). Mingus's work ranged from advanced [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop") and [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz") with small and midsize [ensembles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_band "Jazz band") to pioneering the [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop") style on seminal recordings like _[Pithecanthropus Erectus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pithecanthropus_Erectus_(album) "Pithecanthropus Erectus (album)")_ (1956) and _[Mingus Ah Um](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_Ah_Um "Mingus Ah Um")_ (1959) and [progressive big band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_music#Jazz "Progressive music") experiments such as _[The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Saint_and_the_Sinner_Lady "The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady")_ (1963). Mingus's compositions continue to be played by contemporary musicians ranging from the repertory bands [Mingus Big Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_Big_Band "Mingus Big Band"), [Mingus Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mingus_Dynasty_(band) "Mingus Dynasty (band)"), and Mingus Orchestra to high school students who play the charts and compete in the Charles Mingus High School Competition.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-2) In 1993, the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") acquired Mingus's collected papers—including scores, sound recordings, correspondence, and photos—in what it called "the most important acquisition of a manuscript collection relating to jazz in the Library's history".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-3) ## Biography ### Early life and career Mingus was born in [Nogales, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nogales,_Arizona "Nogales, Arizona"), in 1922, to Charles Mingus Sr., a staff sergeant in the [U.S. Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army"), and Harriet Sophia Mingus (née Phillips). His family moved to the [Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watts,_Los_Angeles "Watts, Los Angeles") area of Los Angeles shortly after his birth.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b13%E2%80%9314-4) Charles Sr. was born in 1877 in [Swain County, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swain_County,_North_Carolina "Swain County, North Carolina"), in the [Great Smoky Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Smoky_Mountains "Great Smoky Mountains"). His mother was a white teenager, Clarinda Mingus; his father was Daniel Mingus, a farmhand and former slave who worked for Clarinda's family. Clarinda married and started a new family when he was six, leaving him in the care of her father and grandparents.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-5) He left home at fourteen, enlisting in the army and seeing action in the [Spanish–American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish%E2%80%93American_War "Spanish–American War"). In 1917, he married Harriet Sophia Phillips, who was of mixed Chinese and African-American descent. She died of [myocarditis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myocarditis "Myocarditis") in 1922, a few months after the birth of their son.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b14%E2%80%9317-6) Mingus was raised alongside his two elder half-sisters, from his father's first marriage. His father was married for a third time in 1923, to Mamie Carson.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-FOOTNOTESantoro2000b18-7) Mamie allowed only [church-related music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_music "Church music") in their home, but Mingus developed an early love for other music, especially that of [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington"). He studied [trombone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trombone "Trombone"), and later [cello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cello "Cello"), although he was unable to follow the cello professionally because, at the time, it was nearly impossible for a black musician to make a career of [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"), and the cello was not accepted as a jazz instrument. Despite this, Mingus remained attached to the cello; as he studied bass with [Red Callender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Callender "Red Callender") in the late 1930s, Callender even commented that the cello was still Mingus's main instrument. In his autobiography, _Beneath the Underdog_, Mingus states that he did not actually start learning bass until [Buddy Collette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_Collette "Buddy Collette") accepted him into his swing band under the stipulation that he be the band's bass player.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Mingus#cite_note-autogenerated1991-8) Due to a poor education, the young Mingus could not read musical notation quickly enough to join the local youth orchestra. This had a serious impact on his early musical experiences, leaving him feeling ostracized from the classical music world.
